item.title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Aishwarya Gavili
item.description: Learn how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that compresses aerospace component substitution evaluation from days to minutes, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the Strands Agents SDK to assemble substitution evidence while keeping the engineer as the decision-maker.
item.content:encoded:
When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check.

A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment.

In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, and the open source Strands Agents SDK. A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own.

Solution overview

The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead.

Three pillars define the architecture:

  • Deterministic spec-fit evaluation – Tolerance-rule code written in Python scores each candidate part against the reference part and the engineer’s stated requirements. Because the same inputs consistently produce the same pass/flag verdicts, the results can go into a formal engineering review.
  • Multi-agent orchestration – A lightweight planner routes each query to one or more of three specialist agents (Catalog, Evaluation, Knowledge), and a supervisor synthesizes their findings only when more than one specialist contributed. Complex questions such as “Check if this wheel is going end-of-life, find alternatives, and score them” chain all three specialists in sequence.
  • Human-in-the-loop decision – The system drafts justification memos and Integration Impact Assessments for engineering review, but it doesn’t recommend or approve a substitution. Every evaluation also writes an audit trail entry aligned with AS9100 sections 8.4 and 8.5.6.

The following diagram shows the architecture.

Figure 1: Architecture of the multi-agent engineering assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. Amazon S3 Vectors is a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A separate fixed chain (Knowledge, then Evaluation, then Supervisor) produces the formal Integration Impact Assessment (IIA) document.

Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings appears in two distinct roles:

  1. Multimodal retrieval – Datasheets, ICDs, and performance charts are embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings so text and visual content share one semantic space. An engineer can enter “torque curve for the 0.06 Nms wheel” or upload a chart image, and retrieval returns the matching diagram with source attribution.
  2. Visual similarity scoring – When two candidate parts are compared, Nova Multimodal Embeddings produces a quantitative cosine similarity between their photos, and Claude analyzes the specific physical differences (mounting pattern, connector placement, housing geometry). The score adds supporting evidence to the deterministic spec comparison, which is what the fit verdict is based on.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region.
  • Model access to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
  • A managed knowledge base created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases, using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings over your parts corpus (datasheets, ICDs, descriptions) for text and document retrieval.
  • An Amazon S3 Vectors index over your part photos and datasheet chart crops, for the image-as-query path.
  • An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector and a managed knowledge base target.
  • Python 3.10 or later and Jupyter for running the notebooks.
  • Docker, if you adapt the deployment recipe in notebook 03 to host the agent on AgentCore runtime.
  • The sample code from the GitHub repository.

Solution walkthrough

The following sections describe each part of the system in the order a query uses it. We start with the parts corpus and the specialist agents, then cover routing, deterministic scoring, the two ways the assistant uses Nova Multimodal Embeddings, the fixed chain that produces formal documents, and deployment to AgentCore runtime.

The complete code sample is a set of five Jupyter notebooks in the GitHub repository, and each notebook runs on its own. The notebooks import from mei_core, a self-contained copy of the agent and tool modules in the same folder, and they include their own parts data, chart crops, and evaluation query set. You can run every snippet in this post from the notebooks without other application code.

Structure the parts corpus

The sample dataset is seven reaction wheels from a fictional manufacturer (AnyCompany) spanning 0.003–5.0 Nms of momentum storage. Each part is a folder that pairs structured data with the source documents an engineer actually reads, and this mix is what makes the corpus multimodal. The specs.json file holds the machine-readable fields that drive deterministic scoring, while the ICD, product photo, and rendered datasheet page carry the visual and narrative detail that structured fields leave out.

data/synthetic-parts-data/rw_rl_0060/
├── specs.json # structured specs + lifecycle fields
├── description.txt # flat text for text retrieval
├── AC-ICD-00068-RW3-0.06-Interface-Control-Document-v2.2.pdf
├── datasheet_page.png # rendered datasheet page
├── datasheet_chart.png # cropped chart region (image-as-query index)
└── photo.png # product image (visual similarity + chart matching)

The specs.json file captures both the engineering specifications and a lifecycle profile, which is what lets the assistant flag obsolescence and lead-time risk alongside spec fit.

{
  "name": "AnyCompany RW3 0.06",
  "category": "reaction_wheel",
  "vendor": "AnyCompany",
  "model": "RW3-0.06",
  "momentum_storage_nms": 0.06,
  "max_torque_mnm": 20,
  "mass_g": 235,
  "voltage_v": "28",
  "voltage_range_v": "7.5 to 36",
  "operating_temp_c": "-30 to +70",
  "interface": "RS-422 or Redundant RS-485",
  "qual_standard": "AnyCompany internal (flight heritage qualified)",
  "lifecycle": {
    "lifecycle_status": "Active",
    "production_status": "Full production",
    "estimated_years_to_eol": "10+",
    "last_time_buy": "Not announced",
    "typical_lead_time_weeks": 10,
    "lead_time_risk": "Low",
    "bathtub_region": "Useful life (highly mature)",
    "recommended_screening": "Standard flight acceptance"
  }
}

The vendor field is stated explicitly for every part. Because catalog folder IDs and file names are reused across datasets, every specialist prompt treats the structured vendor value returned by get_part_specs as authoritative and is forbidden from guessing a manufacturer from an ID, a file name, a photo, or a web search result. Taking the manufacturer from structured data keeps the assistant from attributing a part to the wrong supplier because the model thinks it recognizes the hardware.

Each part folder also carries two assets that text-only indexing cannot use. The product photo feeds visual similarity scoring, and the rendered datasheet page carries torque-box and torque-curve plots that answer performance questions no OCR text layer captures. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings embeds both into the same vector space as the text, so a query can match a spec value, a paragraph, or a plot.

The following sample shows four datasheet pages from the corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage.

Figure 2: Four datasheet pages from the parts corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage

The template repeats across the family, but the product photo and the pair of performance plots change with every part. These Regions show the housing geometry, mounting pattern, torque envelope, and power draw, which the spec fields don’t state directly, so we embed them alongside the text.

Define specialists with scoped tools

Each specialist is a Strands agent with a narrow prompt and only the tools it needs. Scoping tools per specialist keeps behavior predictable, because the Knowledge specialist has no access to the catalog discovery tools and the Catalog specialist has no access to the evaluation tools. The following code creates the Evaluation specialist.

from strands import Agent

def create_evaluation_specialist() -> Agent:
    """Evaluation Specialist: deterministic spec-by-spec comparison and scoring."""
    return Agent(
        name="evaluation_specialist",
        system_prompt="""You are the Evaluation Specialist. Your job is to run
deterministic, spec-driven comparisons between parts.
...
RULES:
- Your comparisons are deterministic (code, not opinion)
- NEVER recommend or approve --- present evidence and flags; the engineer decides
- Always include the disclaimer that this is evidence only""",
        tools=[score_substitution_fit, compare_parts, visual_similarity_score,
               check_qualification_status, generate_substitution_memo],
        model="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5",
    )

The following diagram shows how the planner routes a query to the specialists and when the supervisor synthesizes their results. The list after it describes what each specialist does.

Figure 3: How the planner routes queries to specialists and when the supervisor synthesizes results

  • Catalog – Discovers parts through knowledge base search and exhaustive spec filtering (kb_search, filter_parts_by_spec, get_part_specs, get_substitution_requirements).
  • Evaluation – Scores candidates deterministically and compares parts visually (score_substitution_fit, compare_parts, visual_similarity_score, check_qualification_status, generate_substitution_memo).
  • Knowledge – Answers questions from datasheets and ICDs, checks live end-of-life status, and retrieves visual content (get_part_specs, web_search_eol, retrieve_visual_content).

Use a small model for routing and a large model for synthesis

Routing is a classification task with no tool calls, so it doesn’t need a large reasoning model. A Haiku-based planner returns a numbered routing plan in a couple of seconds. The Opus supervisor runs only when two or more specialists contributed, because synthesizing a single specialist’s already-complete answer adds about 8 seconds of latency with no quality gain.

# Step 1: Planner (fast model) plans the routing (may be multi-step).
plan_response = planner(planning_prompt)
ordered_specialists = _parse_specialist_plan(str(plan_response))

# Step 2: Execute specialists in sequence, passing context forward
accumulated_context = ""
for spec_name in ordered_specialists:
    specialist = specialists[spec_name]
    specialist_response = specialist(spec_prompt)
    accumulated_context += f"\n[{spec_name.upper()}]: {specialist_response}\n"

# Step 3: Synthesize only when 2+ specialists ran.
if len(ordered_specialists) == 1:
    final_text = steps[0]["response"]
else:
    final_text = str(supervisor(synthesis_prompt))

Splitting the work across three model tiers matches cost and latency to each stage. Haiku classifies the query, Sonnet runs the tools, and Opus writes the combined answer, which is the step where response quality matters most.

Keep the scoring deterministic

The spec-fit evaluation runs as ordinary Python code against a hand-written requirements schema. The schema defines the critical specs and tolerance rules for each component category, and score_substitution_fit compares each spec, counts passes and flags, and surfaces lifecycle risk. Because the verdict must be reproducible for an engineering review package, no LLM is involved in this step.

{
  "categories": {
    "reaction_wheel": {
      "critical_specs": [
        {"field": "voltage_v", "label": "Bus voltage (V)",
         "rule": "match", "required_from_user": true},
        {"field": "mass_g", "label": "Mass (g)",
         "rule": "candidate_lte_reference_within_pct", "tolerance_pct": 20,
         "required_from_user": false}
      ]
    }
  }
}

The tool returns a structured verdict with an explicit disclaimer:

return {
    "spec_results": results,  # per-spec pass/flag/review status
    "counts": counts,
    "out_of_tolerance": out_of_tolerance,
    "lifecycle": {...},  # obsolescence and lead-time flags
    "summary": summary,
    "disclaimer": "Evidence only. This tool does not recommend or approve "
                  "a substitution; the engineer decides.",
}

The specialist presents this table and explains the flags, but it can’t change a verdict. The audit trail follows the same division of work. After every evaluation, the orchestration layer reads the specialist’s tool-call history and writes the audit entry itself, so logging doesn’t depend on the model remembering to do it.

Score visual similarity with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings

Form factor matters when a substitute must fit an existing bracket. The visual_similarity_score tool embeds both part photos with Nova Multimodal Embeddings and computes cosine similarity, then asks Claude to describe the specific observable differences.

def embed_image(image_bytes):
    """Embed one image with Nova MME (IMAGE_RETRIEVAL) -> 1024-d vector."""
    b64 = base64.b64encode(image_bytes).decode('utf-8')
    fmt = 'png' if image_bytes[:8] == b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' else 'jpeg'
    body = {
        'taskType': 'SINGLE_EMBEDDING',
        'singleEmbeddingParams': {
            'embeddingPurpose': 'IMAGE_RETRIEVAL',
            'embeddingDimension': 1024,
            'image': {'detailLevel': 'STANDARD_IMAGE', 'format': fmt,
                      'source': {'bytes': b64}},
        },
    }
    resp = bedrock.invoke_model(
        modelId='amazon.nova-2-multimodal-embeddings-v1:0',
        body=json.dumps(body), accept='application/json',
        contentType='application/json',
    )
    result = json.loads(resp['body'].read())
    return np.array(result['embeddings'][0]['embedding'])

# cosine similarity of the two photo embeddings
emb_a, emb_b = embed_image(photo_a_bytes), embed_image(photo_b_bytes)
similarity = float(np.dot(emb_a, emb_b) /
                   (np.linalg.norm(emb_a) * np.linalg.norm(emb_b)))

The embedding similarity is deterministic and reproducible, returning around 0.84 for two wheels of the same product family and 0.40 for wheels of different classes. Claude’s vision analysis then explains what drives the difference, for example noting that one housing is roughly twice the diameter of the other and has a six-hole mounting pattern where the other has four.

Retrieve charts and diagrams with two retrieval paths

Text and document queries go through the managed knowledge base backed by Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through the AgentCore Gateway. Image-as-query (uploading a chart or photo to find matching content) uses a native Amazon S3 Vectors index called directly from the agent, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input.

The Knowledge specialist’s retrieve_visual_content tool provides one interface for both paths. An engineer can paste a performance curve from a requirements document into the chat and ask which part matches it, or describe the chart in a text query instead.

# Image-as-query: embed the uploaded image with Nova MME, exactly as the
# datasheet crops and photos were embedded at indexing time.
def embed_query_image(image_bytes):
    b64 = base64.b64encode(image_bytes).decode('utf-8')
    fmt = 'png' if image_bytes[:8] == b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' else 'jpeg'
    body = {'taskType': 'SINGLE_EMBEDDING', 'singleEmbeddingParams': {
        'embeddingPurpose': 'IMAGE_RETRIEVAL', 'embeddingDimension': 1024,
        'image': {'detailLevel': 'STANDARD_IMAGE', 'format': fmt,
                  'source': {'bytes': b64}}}}
    r = bedrock.invoke_model(modelId=NOVA_MME_MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(body),
                             accept='application/json', contentType='application/json')
    return json.loads(r['body'].read())['embeddings'][0]['embedding']

On the image path, the upload is embedded with Nova Multimodal Embeddings at 1,024 dimensions using the IMAGE_RETRIEVAL purpose, then matched against the S3 Vectors index:

# Query the native S3 Vectors index and collapse to the best vector per part.
emb = embed_query_image(image_bytes)
s3v = boto3.client('s3vectors', region_name=REGION)
fetch_k = max(top_k * 6, 12)  # each part has several vectors; dedupe below
resp = s3v.query_vectors(
    vectorBucketName=S3_VECTOR_BUCKET, indexName=S3_VECTOR_INDEX,
    queryVector={'float32': emb}, topK=fetch_k,
    returnDistance=True, returnMetadata=True,
)

best = {}
for v in resp.get('vectors', []):
    meta = v.get('metadata', {}) or {}
    pid = meta.get('part_id', '')
    if not pid:
        continue
    sim = 1.0 - v.get('distance', 1.0)  # cosine distance -> similarity
    if pid not in best or sim > best[pid]['score']:
        best[pid] = {'part_id': pid, 'score': sim}
ranked = sorted(best.values(), key=lambda r: r["score"], reverse=True)[:top_k]

Because one part contributes several vectors (its photo, the whole datasheet page, and each cropped chart region), results are deduped to the best-scoring vector per part before they reach the model.

We learned three practical lessons while building the retrieval paths:

  • Crop the charts before indexing them – Whole datasheet pages make poor index entries, because roughly 90 percent of a page (header, spec table, footer) is boilerplate that every part shares, and that shared content dominates the embedding. Indexing cropped chart regions alongside the full page solved this. In our testing, chart-upload matching went from 3 of 7 parts correct with whole-page indexing to 7 of 7 with chart-band crops. We define the crop Regions as fractions of the page, which keeps them correct across datasheet resolutions.
  • Filter results when the engineer names a part – Cross-modal text-to-image similarity alone doesn’t reliably return the right part’s chart, because a torque curve image contains no visible part name. When the engineer names a specific part, the tool keeps only results from that part’s indexed content, which it identifies by parsing the part folder out of each result’s S3 URI. Because the filter runs in the tool, it works without custom metadata in the index.
  • Log every fallback on the image path – The image path returns None on errors and falls through to text retrieval. That fallback is reasonable, but it means a missing s3vectors:QueryVectors permission on the AgentCore runtime execution role doesn’t raise an error. Image-as-query stops working without warning, and the model then names a wrong part with high apparent confidence. The problem is easy to miss during development, because local developer credentials usually have broader permissions than the runtime role. The tool now logs an explicit S3 Vectors image query FAILED warning with the bucket, index, and Region whenever that path falls back. Instrument every silent fallback in a retrieval path, because a hard failure is much easier to diagnose than a quiet one.

Produce formal documents with a fixed specialist chain

Chat uses dynamic routing because the right specialists for a freeform question can’t be known in advance. The Integration Impact Assessment works differently. When an engineer requests an impact assessment for a reference and candidate pair, the required sequence is already known, so the service composes the same specialist factory functions in a fixed order with a purpose-built synthesis prompt.

# 1. Knowledge Specialist --- ICD/datasheet interface detail for both parts
knowledge_text = str(knowledge(knowledge_prompt))

# 2. Evaluation Specialist --- structured field delta + qualification check
evaluation_text = str(evaluation(evaluation_prompt))

# Deterministic structured delta for exact summary stats
comparison = compare_parts(reference_id, candidate_id)

# 3. Supervisor --- synthesize into the six-section IIA document
markdown = str(supervisor(synthesis_prompt))

The resulting document covers interface changes, mechanical integration, electrical integration, thermal integration, qualification delta, and supply chain impact. The narrative sections need LLM synthesis, because the pinout and protocol details must be extracted from ICD prose. The summary statistics (matches, differences, total fields) are computed directly from compare_parts output, so the numbers shown alongside the narrative are exact.

Ground lifecycle claims in live web data through AgentCore Gateway

Catalog data goes out of date, so the Knowledge specialist’s web_search_eol tool checks current end-of-life notices, vendor announcements, and lead times through an AgentCore Gateway with the Web Search connector. The Gateway exposes the connector as a governed Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. Because the Gateway also handles managed knowledge base retrieval, you can attach policy and observability to both external and internal data access in one place.

Deploy to AgentCore runtime

For production, you package the agent as an ARM64 container, push it to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and AgentCore runtime hosts it serverlessly with session isolation and auto scaling. Notebook 03 in the GitHub repository walks through this deployment as a reference recipe, covering the Dockerfile, the build and push commands, the execution-role permissions, and the Cedar policy. The notebook shows these steps without running them. Its Dockerfile packages application code that goes beyond the sample, so adapt it to your own application layout before you build. The following diagram shows the deployment path from agent code to a hosted AgentCore runtime endpoint.

Figure 4: Deployment path from agent code to a hosted AgentCore runtime endpoint

export TAG=mei-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
export ACCOUNT=<your-account-id>
export ECR=${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/mfg-engineering-intelligence

# Build the container for ARM64 (required by AgentCore Runtime)
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 -f agentcore/Dockerfile \
  -t mfg-engineering-intelligence:${TAG} --load .

# Push the immutable tag to Amazon ECR
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag mfg-engineering-intelligence:${TAG} ${ECR}:${TAG}
docker push ${ECR}:${TAG}

Give each image an immutable tag. A runtime that has already resolved the digest behind a moving :latest tag keeps serving the old image after you push a new one. Prompt, router, and tool changes all require a new image and a new runtime version to take effect.

The runtime role needs bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:Retrieve, bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway, and s3vectors:QueryVectors for the image-as-query path. The Cedar policy shown in notebook 03 encodes the human-in-the-loop rules, requiring a prior evaluation before memos and an audit log entry on every substitution decision. The application enforces these rules in its own logic today, and attaching the policy to a Cedar authorization engine is the next step.

Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings is now available in AWS GovCloud (US), which matters for aerospace and defense programs subject to data residency, ITAR, and FedRAMP requirements that govern where a workload can run. The multimodal retrieval and visual similarity capabilities this post depends on are reachable inside an AWS GovCloud (US) boundary. Availability of Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore features varies by AWS Region, so check AWS Services by Region before you plan a deployment.

Evaluating the assistant

We measure quality in two ways, with continuous online scoring through AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and offline validation against curated query sets.

AgentCore online evaluation

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, generally available since March 2026, scores agent traces using LLM-as-a-judge techniques. It reads the OpenTelemetry traces that Strands agents already emit, so an instrumented agent needs no application changes to be evaluated. The service offers two modes. Online evaluation continuously samples live production sessions, and on-demand evaluation runs programmatic tests that fit into a continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline.

We use online evaluation, with results published to Amazon CloudWatch for dashboards and alarms. Notebook 05 in the GitHub repository creates an online evaluation configuration and sends test queries to the deployed runtime to generate sessions for scoring.

config = eval_client.create_online_config(
    config_name=CONFIG_NAME,
    agent_id=RUNTIME_ID,
    sampling_rate=SAMPLING_RATE,
    evaluator_list=[
        "Builtin.GoalSuccessRate",
        "Builtin.Correctness",
        "Builtin.Helpfulness",
        "Builtin.Faithfulness",
        "Builtin.ResponseRelevance",
        "Builtin.ToolSelectionAccuracy",
        "Builtin.ToolParameterAccuracy",
    ],
    auto_create_execution_role=True,
    enable_on_create=True,
)

Thirteen built-in evaluators ship with the service, alongside support for custom evaluators defined by a prompt or hosted as an AWS Lambda function. We enable seven, spanning all three scoring levels:

Level Evaluator What it scores
Session Goal Success Rate Did the conversation achieve the user’s goal end to end?
Trace Correctness Is the information factually accurate?
Trace Helpfulness Is the response useful and valuable?
Trace Faithfulness Is the response faithful to the retrieved context?
Trace Response Relevance Does the response address the user’s actual query?
Tool call Tool Selection Accuracy Did the agent pick the right tool?
Tool call Tool Parameter Accuracy Did the agent extract parameters correctly?

The curated query set holds 36 queries across six categories: catalog discovery (8), Knowledge and ICD retrieval (8), multi-specialist chains (6), deterministic evaluation (5), text-to-visual retrieval (5), and human-in-the-loop safety refusals (4) that assert the agent refuses to recommend or approve. Each query carries its expected catalog part IDs, except the safety queries, where the expected outcome is a refusal.

export AGENTCORE_RUNTIME_ARN=arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:ACCOUNT:runtime/YOUR_RUNTIME
jupyter lab 05_evaluation.ipynb

Results

AgentCore samples live sessions on an ongoing basis, so each evaluator’s score is a moving aggregate that shifts as traffic accumulates and as the agent changes. The following numbers are a snapshot from the synthetic dataset run. Use them as a baseline for setting CloudWatch alarm thresholds, and expect the numbers from your own runs to differ.

Level Evaluator Score (30-day avg)
Session Goal Success Rate 0.892
Trace Correctness 0.968
Trace Helpfulness 0.956
Trace Faithfulness 0.981
Trace Response Relevance 0.968
Tool call Tool Selection Accuracy 0.861
Tool call Tool Parameter Accuracy 0.980

All trace-level quality metrics scored at or above 0.95, and tool parameter extraction was near-perfect at 0.980. The most notable improvement between evaluation runs was Tool Selection Accuracy, which rose from 0.809 to 0.861. Three changes drove the gain: consolidating to a single managed knowledge base, fixing a missing permission on the image-as-query path that had caused silent fallback to text search, and tightening the planner’s routing to avoid chaining unnecessary specialists.

Goal Success Rate is lower, at 0.892, because of how the query set is designed. The query set includes safety-category prompts that ask the agent to recommend or approve a substitution. The agent correctly refuses, but the evaluator scores a correct refusal as an unmet goal. We expect this result, because in a human-in-the-loop system the agent must not approve a substitution on its own.

Adapt the pattern to your own catalog

The code is a reusable pattern that works for other part categories, beyond reaction wheels. Swapping domains requires three changes: replace the parts data (a specs.json, description, ICD, datasheet page, and photo per part), edit the requirements schema to define your category’s critical specs and tolerance rules, and point the knowledge base at your S3 corpus. The agents, tools, and scoring engine carry over unchanged. Because the deterministic tools in mei_core are plain Python functions, a PLM or ERP integration can call score_substitution_fit directly, with no agent in the loop.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created:

  1. Delete the AgentCore runtime agent and its Amazon ECR repository.
  2. Delete the AgentCore Gateway and its Web Search and knowledge base targets.
  3. Delete the online evaluation configuration and the CloudWatch alarms you created.
  4. Delete the managed knowledge base and the S3 Vectors index.
  5. Delete the S3 bucket holding the parts corpus.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that replaces manual part substitution research with automated evidence assembly. The architecture pairs Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, which handles visual similarity scoring and chart retrieval that text-only systems miss, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which provides the production scaffolding of runtime hosting, Gateway-governed retrieval and web search, and quality evaluations. Three design choices matter most. Deterministic code produces every pass/fail verdict, each task runs on the smallest of the three model tiers that handles it well, and only the engineer can approve a substitution.

To get started, clone the GitHub repository, run the notebooks with your own AWS account, and swap in your parts catalog and requirements schema. To go deeper on the retrieval foundations, read Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and A practical guide to Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings. For production agent patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the Strands Agents SDK.

item.title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
item.dc:creator: Marek Klatowicz
item.description: Circle K's DevOps team cut incident triage from 45-60 minutes to under 15 by building an agentic triage system on Amazon Bedrock. This post walks through the architecture, the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation, the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the lessons learned from scaling it.
item.content:encoded:
This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K.

Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin.

At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin.

To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock, a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened.

Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics.

In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and share lessons learned from scaling the system.

The challenge of triage overhead

Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context.

When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch, examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service, checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded.

The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently.

Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation.

Why Circle K chose Amazon Bedrock

The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls.

With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. They could access foundation models through a single API and swap foundation models without rewriting code. Because Circle K already ran on AWS, Amazon Bedrock fit into existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations, and logging pipelines.

Two managed capabilities covered orchestration and retrieval. Amazon Bedrock helped with agent orchestration, giving the agents native tool use to call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents without custom orchestration code. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handled ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards, so the team did not need to run a separate vector database. This let the DevOps team focus on prompt design and tool definitions.

Data privacy completed the picture. Circle K’s incident data includes operational metrics, infrastructure details, and logs that can contain sensitive information. Amazon Bedrock does not share customer data with model providers or use it to train foundation models. For a team feeding production logs and internal service details into the system, this data handling approach met Circle K’s security requirements.

Solution overview

This section describes the initial architecture, which the team built on Amazon Bedrock Flows. A later section covers the migration to AgentCore.

The solution uses Amazon Bedrock Flows as the orchestration layer, coordinating a set of specialized agents that each handle a different part of the analysis. The pipeline starts when a Grafana alert publishes a notification to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), which forwards it to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. An AWS Lambda function polls the queue, extracts the alert payload, and invokes the Flow.

Inside the Flow, two agents are invoked in parallel. The AWSResourceExplorerAgent queries infrastructure across multiple workload accounts managed with AWS Organizations. It checks Amazon ECS task status, Application Load Balancer target health, and CloudWatch metrics and logs. At the same time, the OpenSearchExplorerAgent queries Amazon OpenSearch Service for application-level logs and distributed traces. This agent runs separately because OpenSearch returns large volumes of log data. Isolating it keeps each agent’s context window manageable. It also has exclusive access to the knowledge base, which contains product cards describing each service and its dependencies.

After both agents return their findings, the GitHubExplorerAgent runs. It receives output from the previous two agents and finds the affected service’s GitHub repositories. Then it searches their application code, infrastructure definitions, and recent commits to pinpoint the source of the problem and propose a concrete fix. Running it after the parallel agents means it knows exactly what to search for rather than performing a broad query.

All three outputs feed into an AnalysisPrompt node, which is a single model call with no tools attached. It receives the AWS resource data, the OpenSearch logs, and the GitHub context, then produces a structured summary: probable root cause, supporting evidence, affected service and owner, and recommended remediation steps. The prompt output uses a consistent format that the on-call team can scan in under 2 minutes.

The Flow returns this summary to the invoking Lambda function, which posts it to a Slack channel. The entire process from alert to Slack message takes 5–15 minutes depending on incident complexity.

The following diagram shows this architecture end to end, from the initial Grafana alert to the final Slack summary.

Figure 1: Circle K automated incident triage architecture using Amazon Bedrock Flows

Example triage

A Grafana alert: HTTP 5xx error rate on a service exceeds 5% for 3 consecutive minutes.

The AWSResourceExplorerAgent checks ECS task health in the target account and finds the database connection pool exhausted, with the ECS service attempting restarts. The OpenSearchExplorerAgent returns application logs showing “connection refused” errors from the service to its backing PostgreSQL database. It also retrieves the product card for the affected service from the knowledge base, which documents its dependency on that database. The GitHubExplorerAgent searches the service’s repository and infrastructure files and finds the Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) definition. It sees that the service opens a new database connection per request rather than reusing existing ones.

The AnalysisPrompt receives all three results. It correlates the timing with a scheduled marketing campaign that started 10 minutes before the alert. It combines that with the GitHubExplorerAgent’s finding to recommend a concrete code-level fix rather than a temporary patch.

The final Slack message reads:

Summary: XYZ Service 5xx errors caused by connection pool exhaustion
Root cause: Scheduled marketing campaign drove traffic spike; connection pool max (50) insufficient for load
Evidence: OpenSearch logs show "connection refused" at 14:32 UTC; ECS shows 3 task restarts since 14:30
Owner: XYZ team (backend)
Next steps: Add Amazon RDS Proxy to pool connections, or update the service to reuse existing connections instead of opening a new one per request; consider an Auto Scaling rule for future campaigns

Scaling to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

The Amazon Bedrock Flows architecture worked well for months, and simple incidents were triaged in under 10 minutes. Over time, the volume of data and the context behind each investigation grew, even though the set of services stayed the same. Some incidents required longer-running analysis than a single Flow node could complete.

The team first optimized within the existing design by filtering logs more aggressively, shortening context windows, and splitting certain services into separate Flows. These steps helped, but log volumes and the knowledge base kept growing.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore met this need. AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. For this workload, the key capability was AgentCore Runtime: The full investigation runs in a single session, so each step can take the time its data requires. AgentCore Runtime supports sessions of up to 8 hours, well beyond what the current investigations need. The team containerized their agent logic and deployed it on AgentCore Runtime.

The following diagram shows the production architecture after the move to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Figure 2: Production architecture using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and AgentCore Gateway

The analysis logic stays the same, but the way it runs has changed. The three specialized agents from the Flows version are now consolidated into a single agent running in an AgentCore Runtime session. The Lambda function starts the session, and the agent performs the same steps as before. It queries AWS resources across accounts, pulls logs from Amazon OpenSearch Service, searches GitHub, and retrieves product cards from the knowledge base. The agent returns its findings to the Lambda function within 15 minutes, which is within the maximum Lambda timeout. The Lambda function then posts the structured summary to Slack.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, brokers the agent’s access to its data sources, including Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and GitHub. The Gateway exposes each source as a tool the agent invokes, which centralizes access control and makes it simpler for the team to add or change data sources.

How AgentCore Runtime supported the team’s growing scale

Beyond longer-running sessions, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime added three capabilities that supported the team’s growing scale: session persistence, OpenTelemetry-based observability, and framework flexibility.

Session persistence: The agent keeps an intermediate state throughout an investigation. If a first pass over the logs surfaces something, the agent can run a second, more targeted pass without losing the context it has already built. This fits the iterative way that complex, multi-service incidents are investigated.

Observability: AgentCore captures traces from each session using OpenTelemetry standards and surfaces through CloudWatch. The team can see how long each step takes, which knowledge base queries the agent makes, and where bottlenecks occur. These insights feed directly into prompt tuning.

Framework flexibility: With AgentCore Runtime, the team can deploy containerized agents built with a wide range of frameworks. They can iterate agent logic, add triage steps, or restructure the agent’s reasoning as their requirements change, all on the same Runtime.

The AgentCore architecture now runs in production and handles the full range of incidents, from simple single-service alerts to large multi-service investigations.

Results

Circle K deployed the AgentCore version of the triage system in April 2026. Based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics, mean triage time dropped from 45–60 minutes to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction. Straightforward incidents receive a summary in 5–8 minutes. Complex multi-service incidents, which previously took more than an hour to triage manually, now complete within 15 minutes.

Engineers now start from a summary instead of gathering context themselves. The team sees three changes in how incidents are handled:

Consistent triage. Every on-call engineer receives the same structured summary, with the same log excerpts, knowledge base references, and recommended next steps, regardless of how well they know the affected service.

Faster escalation. When an issue requires support from another team, the summary gives the on-call engineer the relevant context for a timely, informed escalation.

Quicker handling of false alarms. When the analysis finds healthy services and no correlated errors, the engineer can acknowledge the alert and move on.

Lessons learned

Building this system took several iterations. Four lessons stood out that apply to teams building a similar solution with Amazon Bedrock.

Include log content directly in the prompt. Early versions passed only log group names and time ranges, then the agent attempted to query CloudWatch through action groups. This added latency and often returned too much data to process. Circle K got better results by having Lambda functions pre-query the logs and pass relevant lines directly to the agent. The agent reasons faster when it can read the actual error messages.

Tune retrieval and generation for use cases. Retrieval configuration significantly affected result quality from the knowledge base. After testing the available options, the Circle K team found that an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with its default configuration worked best for their data. Amazon Bedrock handles embeddings, indexing, and vector storage end to end, so the team has fewer components to maintain. On the generation side, a well-designed system prompt and a tuned temperature setting produced consistent summaries in Slack.

Narrow the code search with findings from the logs. Searching for the service’s repositories without a lead returns too many results to be useful. The team runs the GitHub search after the AWS resource and log analysis, so the agent already knows which error, component, or recent change to look for. In the example triage, this is how the agent found that the service opened a new database connection for every request.

Keep the analysis logic independent of the orchestration layer. Analysis time grows with data volume, so plan for investigations to take longer over time. The team kept its prompts, tool definitions, and analysis steps separate from the flow structure. This made it possible to consolidate them into a single agent on AgentCore Runtime without rewriting the triage logic.

Next steps

Today, the triage system finds the probable root cause and recommends a fix, and an engineer carries out the fix. Next, the team plans to integrate with AWS DevOps Agent, so the system can also handle simple remediations. Examples include restarting a task, scaling up a service, or rolling back a deployment. An engineer will approve each action in Slack before it runs.

The team also plans to give the agent more context to work with:

  • Jira, to link each incident to related tickets and track follow-up work.
  • Confluence, to add internal documentation to the code and logs the agent already reads.
  • Runbooks in the knowledge base, so the agent can match symptoms to known failure modes and fixes that worked before, instead of relying on product cards alone.

Conclusion

The Circle K team went from 45–60 minutes of manual incident triage to under 15 minutes by automating the context gathering that engineers used to do by hand. The system collects data from logs, AWS resources, and code, lets an agent reason over it, and delivers a structured summary to Slack.

The team built the first version on Amazon Bedrock Flows and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. As investigations grew larger, the team moved to a single agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, with AgentCore Gateway providing access to its data sources.

If your team spends most of its incident response time gathering context rather than fixing problems, this pattern applies directly. To get started, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. For hands-on guidance or to discuss your use case with an AWS specialist, visit the Amazon Bedrock getting started page or contact AWS.

We want to hear how you approach incident triage. Share your experience in the comments.

Marek is a Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K, where he works with AWS to design and improve cloud services for enterprise end customers. Lately he has spent much of his time on AI, building solutions that deliver real business value. He believes in simple solutions that just work.

Sefat is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, where she helps enterprise customers build AI-powered operational tooling on AWS. She specializes in generative AI applications, agent architectures, and DevOps automation. Outside of work, she enjoys experimenting with cooking, music, and home automation projects.

item.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
item.dc:creator: Aswath Ram A Srinivasan
item.description: This post presents a five-stage operating model for managing Amazon Bedrock cost: attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, enforce budgets, optimize platform defaults, and operate a review cadence. Written for FinOps and platform engineering teams.
item.content:encoded:
Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?

Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.

The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.

In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.

The operating model in one view

Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.

Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop

Stage 1: Attribute every dollar

You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0, and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.

Setup is four steps:

  1. Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.
  2. Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.
  3. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus API).
  4. Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix (for example, iamPrincipal/team) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.

This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.

The shared-role problem

The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).

This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is line_item_iam_principal entries like assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex, each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.

import boto3

sts = boto3.client("sts")

# One call per user; cache the returned credentials up to 1 hour
response = sts.assume_role(
    RoleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/BedrockRuntimeRole",
    RoleSessionName="gw-alex", # the user, not the gateway
    Tags=[
        {"Key": "team", "Value": "sales-ai"},
        {"Key": "application", "Value": "renewal-agent"},
        {"Key": "costCenter", "Value": "CC-2041"}
    ]
)

A note on application inference profiles and Projects

Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the bedrock-mantle endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.

For bedrock-runtime workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for bedrock-mantle workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.

Stage 2: Make every request observable

CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.

Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes (Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).

Request metadata for workload-level attribution

Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:

The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

response = client.converse(
    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5",
    messages=[...],
    requestMetadata={
        "application": "renewal-copilot",
        "workflow": "renewal-risk-summary",
        "tenant": "enterprise-sales",
        "agent": "renewal-agent"
    }
)

Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.

Diagnostic queries

With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens:

fields @timestamp, identity.arn as caller, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inTokens,
output.outputTokenCount as outTokens
| stats sum(inTokens + outTokens) as totalTokens,
count(*) as calls
by caller, modelId
| sort totalTokens desc
| limit 25

The same query grouped by requestMetadata.application and requestMetadata.workflow instead of caller produces the workload-level leaderboard: the view product and engineering teams will ask FinOps for the moment chargeback conversations start.

Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.

Stage 3: Enforce budgets

With attribution and observability in place, enforcement becomes an architecture choice rather than a wish. There are three viable tiers. The right one depends on your spend velocity, your risk tolerance for overspend, and how your tools connect to Amazon Bedrock.

Tier 1: Monitor and alert (no blocking)

Amazon Bedrock writes principal identity into the billing pipeline automatically. You put AWS Budgets on top for threshold alerts, with the OpenTelemetry dashboards from Stage 2 closing the 24-hour CUR gap for day-to-day visibility. Nothing to deploy, native AWS billing, and no added latency on inference calls. It works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. Nothing can hard-stop spend, so you see the problem after it happens. Right for early adoption, where alerting plus human intervention is sufficient. Two builder guides walk through it: Limiting Bedrock usage and controlling costs, and Deep dive on managing Bedrock in Claude Code with AWS Budgets and Tags.

Tier 2: IAM tag enforcement (deny on breach)

An aggregator AWS Lambda function tallies per-user token and dollar counters in Amazon DynamoDB from invocation log data. When a user breaches their threshold, the function adds their identity to a shared IAM deny policy (denying bedrock:*) until a monthly reset or admin override. This enforcement runs entirely on IAM and Amazon Bedrock logging, with no third-party component in the inference path, and it works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. The Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Solutions Library provides a deployable variant. It checks each user’s usage against per-user and per-team limits when it issues credentials, and withholds credentials once a user exceeds their limit. Because that check uses usage telemetry emitted by the client, its figures can differ from CUR. In either form, enforcement is asynchronous. A block takes effect seconds to minutes after the breaching call for an IAM policy update, or at the next credential refresh for the credential check. Your platform team owns the pipeline. This tier is right for teams that need real enforcement, can tolerate that lag, and want to keep third-party software out of the data path.

Tier 3: Gateway enforcement (synchronous block)

A gateway sits in the inference data path and enforces budgets synchronously, returning HTTP 429 the moment a user or team exceeds their limit. You get sub-second blocking, per-user model allowlists, token rate limits, and centrally enforced routing rules. The trade-off: a component in the data path that must be deployed, scaled, and security-reviewed. Clients must be configured to send their requests through the gateway.

For Claude Code and Claude Desktop fleets, the Claude apps gateway for AWS is the official recommendation. It ships inside the CLI binary and runs as a single stateless container backed by PostgreSQL. It provides OIDC identity, centrally managed policy, OpenTelemetry telemetry, multi-Region Amazon Bedrock routing, and per-user/group/org spend caps out of the box. For mixed-model workloads spanning multiple providers, general-purpose gateways remain the right choice: LiteLLM through the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate reference architecture, or a serverless alternative described in Build a proactive AI cost management system for Amazon Bedrock, Part 2.

Choosing a tier

Two factors dominate.

Connectivity: If developers call Amazon Bedrock directly with no proxy, only Tiers 1 and 2 are viable.

Spend velocity: If spend is already in the millions per month, build enforcement now. If alerts can hold the line for another quarter, invest in Stages 1 and 2 first and add enforcement when the data demands it.

Most organizations should phase it: observe at Tier 1, then step up. Treat all three as bridges, not destinations: the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens already codifies agent cost governance as a first-class architectural concern, and the attribution foundation from Stage 1 is what any managed enforcement will sit on.

Stage 4: Optimize the defaults

Most Amazon Bedrock waste is not individual carelessness. It is platform defaults nobody set. The two highest-impact levers are both platform-controlled.

Model routing

Not every task needs a frontier model. Routine completions (boilerplate, linting suggestions, small refactors) can run on smaller, cheaper models with quality reserved for complex reasoning, through intelligent prompt routing within a model family or routing rules at the gateway (see Reduce costs and latency with Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing and prompt caching for the full walkthrough). Which workflows can downshift is an empirical question: pull the workload leaderboard from Stage 2, run a quality evaluation on the cheaper model for the top entries, and route what passes. For agentic coding fleets, where boilerplate dominates call volume, more than half of calls landing on cheaper models is an achievable target.

Prompt caching

Prompt caching rewards stable repeated prefixes. As of October 2026, the published Amazon Bedrock pricing for Anthropic Claude models in US East (N. Virginia) bills a cache write at 1.25x the base input rate with the 5-minute time-to-live (TTL) (2x with the 1-hour TTL). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input rate on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and at 0.05x on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Check the pricing page for your model and Region, because these multipliers vary by model and can change. The break-even math is friendlier than teams assume. With the 5-minute TTL, a single reuse already pays for the write, and ten calls against a stable prefix cost roughly a fifth of the uncached price (about 22 percent at a 0.1x read rate, 17 percent at 0.05x). The only losing case is writes that are never re-read, which cost 25 percent extra with the 5-minute TTL and double with the 1-hour TTL. So the platform dashboard should track cache-read volume against cache-write volume per workflow. A low read ratio means the prefix is not actually stable (usually a timestamp or session ID embedded before the cache point).

Candidates surface directly from the invocation logs:

fields requestMetadata.workflow as workflow, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inTokens
| stats count(*) as calls,
avg(inTokens) as avgInputTokens,
sum(inTokens) as totalInputTokens
by workflow, modelId
| filter calls > 50 and avgInputTokens > 2000
| sort totalInputTokens desc
| limit 25

Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.

Application-level optimization

A third class of savings (just-in-time retrieval instead of stuffed context, compaction of long conversations, distilling stable high-volume workflows onto smaller models) belongs to application teams rather than the platform. The platform’s job is to make those savings visible: publish the per-workflow token leaderboard, set token limits per model and workflow, and let the teams that own expensive workflows see exactly where they stand.

Stage 5: Operate the loop

The first four stages produce data. This one turns it into decisions. The platform team runs a standing health dashboard with four signals:

  • Model mix: Which models are called and how often, the direct measure of routing discipline.
  • Failed request rates: Errors, throttles, and timeouts. Each retry adds latency, and a client-side timeout on a request that still completes on the service side can be billed twice, once for the abandoned call and once for the retry.
  • Cache effectiveness: The read-versus-write ratio from Stage 4.
  • Metadata coverage: The percentage of production calls with complete metadata. Every uncovered call is an attribution blind spot that quietly degrades every other number.

When a signal drifts, the remediation is a policy change (routing rules, token limits, metadata enforcement), not an email asking teams to be careful.

The money loop

FinOps runs the money loop on the same data. When attribution is clean, anomaly detection becomes an investigation stream rather than a panicked all-hands: a spike in a tagged team or application triggers a lookup in the Stage 2 leaderboard, not a war room. Chargeback runs from CUR groupings by team and application.

Scorecard

The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and pricing tier before adopting them as policy.

Dimension Metric Green Yellow Red
Unit economics Cost per successful outcome ≤ budget 1–1.5x budget >1.5x budget
Per-dev cost Daily spend per developer <$100 $100–$300 >$300
Model routing % of calls to cost-efficient-models >50% 30–50% <30%
Cache efficiency Cache-read hit ratio >60% 30–60% <30%

Green means the workload operates inside its economic envelope. Yellow means routing or caching discipline is slipping. Red means spend is concentrating in premium models or uncached context, and the Stage 3 and 4 controls are the remediation path. Review this scorecard on a regular cadence (weekly for high-velocity fleets, biweekly otherwise) and treat it as the joint FinOps-plus-platform decision surface.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build a five-stage operating model that takes Amazon Bedrock spend from uncontrolled to fully governed:

  1. Attribute every dollar to an owner using IAM principal tags, session tags, and CUR 2.0.
  2. Observe every request through model invocation logging and stamped request metadata.
  3. Enforce budgets at the tier that matches your risk: monitor-only, IAM deny on breach, or synchronous gateway blocking.
  4. Optimize platform defaults with intelligent prompt routing and prompt caching to remove waste centrally.
  5. Operate a scorecard and review cadence that turns telemetry into policy decisions.

Notice the first row of that scorecard: cost per successful outcome, not cost per call. That distinction is where this playbook hands off. Everything here makes Amazon Bedrock spend visible, attributable, capped, and efficient, but a workflow can be perfectly efficient and still not be worth running. Deciding that requires measuring the agent against the human process it replaced, which is a product and analytics discipline rather than a FinOps one. What the cost platform contributes is the foundation: clean attribution and per-workflow cost data are exactly the inputs that outcome measurement joins against.

Build the five stages and you can answer, end to end: who spent it, why, and whether it was controlled. That is what it means to manage Amazon Bedrock cost, and it is the difference between a monthly bill review and an operating model.

To get started, deploy the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock reference architecture for Stages 1–3, then use the cost attribution best practices documentation to configure your tagging strategy.
