item.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
item.dc:creator: Sundar Raghavan
item.description: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Session endpoints give each runtime session an authenticated URL that forwards any HTTP method, path, and WebSocket connection to the ports you allow. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then watch the live site update in your browser as the agent edits files.
item.content:encoded:
Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints, you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.

In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.

The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

How Session endpoints work

Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.

You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime: 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports. Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0.

The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl.

Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer, each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.

The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:

https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html
https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status

It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.

It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting.

A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088, and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.

A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint, which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as DEFAULT, to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. InvokeAgentRuntime calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.

Solution overview

The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, PreviewApp serves the preview page, sends your prompts to InvokeAgentRuntime, and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through InvokeAgentRuntime to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.

Figure 1: Solution architecture

Before step 1, PreviewApp has already called InvokeAgentRuntime once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. PreviewApp read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:

  1. The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on localhost:8088. The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against allowedPorts, then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.
  2. You send a prompt from the chat pane. PreviewApp sends it to InvokeAgentRuntime as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.
  3. The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.
  4. The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.
  5. When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.
  6. From the notebook, PreviewApp reads the agent’s /status route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.

Port 8080 isn’t in allowedPorts, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.

Prerequisites

To follow the walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.
  • Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and create a runtime, plus bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on that runtime and its DEFAULT runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime.
  • Python 3.10 or later, with bedrock-agentcore 1.25.2 or later and boto3 1.43.122 or later.
  • Git, to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.
  • Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models.
  • Node.js 22 or later with npm, which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.

The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js, so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.

Deploy the agent and its website

First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.

The following excerpt from deploy.py shows the two settings that matter for this post. protocolConfiguration says where the agent listens for InvokeAgentRuntime, and allowedPorts lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path.

agentRuntimeArtifact={"codeConfiguration": {
    "code": {"s3": {"bucket": code_bucket(), "prefix": S3_PREFIX}},
    "runtime": "NODE_22",
    "entryPoint": ["app.js"],
}},
protocolConfiguration={"serverProtocol": "HTTP", "port": 8080, "path": "/invocations"},
allowedPorts=[{"port": 8090}, {"port": 8081}],

The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 0.0.0.0 at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the Host header (server.allowedHosts is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather than localhost. The Session endpoint authenticates every request before it reaches the server, so the server doesn’t need its own host check.

To deploy the runtime:

1. Clone the sample repo and change to the sample folder:

git clone https://github.com/awslabs/agentcore-samples.git
cd agentcore-samples/01-features/02-host-your-agent/01-runtime/03-advanced/16-session-endpoints

2. Open session_endpoints_preview.ipynb from the sample folder.

3. Run the install cell, which installs the Python dependencies.

4. Run the %run deploy.py cell. Deployment takes a few minutes, mostly waiting for the runtime to reach the READY status.

Open the preview

With the runtime ready, you start the preview. One call does three things: it starts a session (which starts the website), opens a local endpoint for port 8090, and serves the preview page on localhost:8087.

from preview_app import PreviewApp

app = PreviewApp().start()
print("Open", app.url)

Inside start(), the calls that use Session endpoints are short. The first InvokeAgentRuntime call returns the URL in a response header, session_endpoint_url reads it, and the Session endpoint client opens a local endpoint for port 8090:

answer = client.invoke_agent_runtime(
    agentRuntimeArn=runtime_arn, runtimeSessionId=session_id,
    payload=json.dumps({"prompt": ""}).encode(), contentType="application/json",
)
endpoint = client.session_endpoint_client(session_endpoint_url(answer))
local = endpoint.open_local_endpoint(port=8090, local_port=8088).start()

To open the preview:

  1. Run the cell that starts PreviewApp.
  2. Open the printed link, http://localhost:8087, in your browser.

The page shows the website on the right, served from port 8090 in the session, and a short guide with suggested requests on the left.

Ask the agent for a change

Now you ask for a change and watch it arrive. Each prompt goes to the agent through InvokeAgentRuntime. The agent reads the files it needs, writes the ones it changes, and reports each step as it happens. When a file is saved, the Vite development server pushes the change over its WebSocket, through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the website updates in place.

To ask for a change:

  1. On the preview page, choose Switch this website to a dark coffee-house color theme.
  2. Follow the agent’s steps in the chat pane as it reads and saves files.
  3. Watch the site pane. It changes when the agent saves the stylesheet, and a banner names the file the change came from.

The following video shows the preview page while the agent works through several requests. Choosing a suggested request sends it to the agent, the chat pane lists each file the agent reads and saves, and the site pane on the right updates without a refresh, from the dark theme to a green Order ahead button.

Figure 2: The preview page as the agent works

The steps stream because the agent answers with server-sent events when you ask it to. You can send the same prompts from Python with app.ask, which reads the stream with iter_events from the bedrock-agentcore SDK. The open page updates in the same way:

for event in app.ask("Make the Order ahead button green"):
    if "step" in event:
        print("  ", event["step"])
    elif "done" in event:
        print(event["done"]["reply"])

The output of this Python script should resemble the following:

   Looking at the site's files
   Reading src/main.js
   Reading src/style.css
   Reading index.html
   Saved src/style.css
The Order ahead button is now green instead of brown, with white text kept for contrast. You can see it in the hero section, just below the "Small batch coffee, roasted every morning" heading at the top of the page.

Reach a second port in the same session

The website isn’t the only server you can reach. The agent serves /status on port 8081, which lists each prompt and the files it changed. The same Session endpoint reaches it, and the only difference is the port argument.

status = app.endpoint.request("GET", "/status", port=8081)
print("GET /status on port 8081: HTTP", status.status)
for edit in status.json()["edits"]:
    print("  ", edit["prompt"], "->", ", ".join(edit["files"]))

The output of this Python script should resemble the following:

GET /status on port 8081: HTTP 200
   Make the Order ahead button green -> src/style.css

What the Session endpoint refuses

When the runtime refuses a request, it answers with an HTTP status, an empty body, and an error code in a response header, so you can tell its refusals from errors your application returns. The notebook sends a request to a port outside allowedPorts and a request without credentials, and the runtime refuses both with 403 AccessDenied.

The following table lists the refusals you’re likely to meet while you build with Session endpoints.

Request Response from the runtime
A port that isn’t in allowedPorts 403 AccessDenied
A request without valid credentials 403 AccessDenied or 401 AuthenticationRequired
An allowed port with nothing listening on it 502 PortNotReachable
A URL whose session no longer exists 404 SessionNotFound

How access to your session is protected

The runtime removes its own authentication headers before it forwards a request, so the website doesn’t receive your signature. Requests are recorded in AWS CloudTrail as InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy events, with the event source bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com. The local endpoint acts with your credentials, so it limits who can use it. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers only requests addressed to its own local address, and refuses WebSocket connections opened by pages from other origins. Run the local endpoint only while you use the preview. For more information, see Log session endpoint requests in CloudTrail.

The access controls don’t separate the website from the agent. Both run in the same session, so give the execution role only the permissions the agent needs. If the runtime replaces the session’s compute, open connections close, and the agent’s edits might not survive unless the session uses persistent storage. Refer to File system configurations for AgentCore runtime if you need the files to outlast the compute.

The agent’s file tools resolve every path inside the site folder and refuse paths outside it, so a prompt can’t make the agent change other files in the session. If other people can send prompts to your coding agent, consider Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful prompts and responses, and review the agent’s changes before you publish them.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, stop the preview and delete the resources the sample created. The website the agent edited lives in the session, so it goes with the session.

To clean up:

1. Run the stop cell, and press Enter when the notebook asks. This stops the preview page, the local endpoint, and the session.

2. Run the %run cleanup.py cell, which deletes the runtime, the uploaded code, and the IAM role.

Conclusion

Session endpoints give you authenticated access to the applications in an AgentCore runtime session from your own tools over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and WebSocket, on the ports you allow. In this post, you deployed a coding agent with a Vite website in its session, opened the live website in your browser through a local endpoint, asked the agent for a dark theme, and watched the change arrive as the agent saved the file. You also reached a second port in the same session and confirmed what the Session endpoint refuses.

To go further, run the notebook with your own site in the site folder, or change the agent’s tools to match how your coding agent works. For the full set of options, including port ranges, OAuth, HTTP/2, and gRPC, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint.

To change the port or path that InvokeAgentRuntime uses in your own agent, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path. If your agent also needs to run build or test commands in the same session, refer to Execute shell commands in AgentCore runtime sessions. To deploy your own Node.js agent from a zip file the way this sample does, refer to Direct code deployment for Node.js. For everything else the service offers, start with Host agent or tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and find more examples in the agentcore-samples GitHub repo.

He leads the developer experience for Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is also bringing the same agent developer experience to Physical AI through Strands Robots.

item.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
item.dc:creator: Saumya Shah
item.description: Worldwide Express automated its less-than-truckload freight billing-exception process with a multi-agent solution built on Amazon Bedrock. Six months after launch, the company cut active exceptions by 75%, improved time-to-cash by four weeks, and unlocked $10 million in free cash flow.
item.content:encoded:
Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.

Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.

In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.

The challenge

In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:

  • Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
  • Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
  • Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.

Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:

  1. Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
  2. Research the root cause in vendor records.
  3. Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
  4. Wait for a response.
  5. Execute the resolution in the TMS.

With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.

Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.

From assessment to production

In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.

How it works

The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.

Agents

When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:

  • Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
  • Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
  • Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.

Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.

Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

Actions

The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.

Carrier knowledge base

Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.

Human-in-the-loop

The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.

Observability

Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.

End-to-end flow

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.

Figure 1: Worldwide Express’s AI-powered exception handling architecture on AWS

Results

Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.

The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.

“With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”

— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express

Looking forward

Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.

Conclusion

Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.

To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock. Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

item.dc:creator: Virgil Ennes
item.description: The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). This post walks through a controlled local deployment that routes model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West) using API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions, so a security team can validate it before broader use.
item.content:encoded:
The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.

This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1, where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.

Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.

For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.

This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.

Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.

Solution overview

You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:

  • Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
  • Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.

The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1. Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.

Walkthrough

The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.

Prerequisites

Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files.

Step 1: Set up authentication

Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1. Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile codex-il5. Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.

Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.

The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain. AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.

The app first checks for AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through %USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env on Windows or ~/.codex/.env on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.

If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials and related profile settings from ~/.aws/config. On Windows, the corresponding default paths are %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\config. The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation.

Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files

You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: config.toml and requirements.toml.

Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.

Operating system User config.toml Admin requirements.toml
Windows %USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml
Linux ~/.codex/config.toml /etc/codex/requirements.toml
macOS ~/.codex/config.toml /etc/codex/requirements.toml

Start from the requirements.toml file. requirements.toml is an administrator-controlled rules file. It sets security limits that users can’t override, for example, restricting which permission levels, tools, or settings the ChatGPT desktop app is allowed to use.

Use the following baseline for the supported AWS GovCloud (US) Amazon Bedrock deployment. The [windows] section applies only to Windows, and sandbox_private_desktop must be supported by the approved runtime.

mcp_elicitations = false, request_permissions = false,
skill_approval = true } },
]

browser_use_full_cdp_access = false

in_app_updates = false
image_generation = false

guardian_approval = false
guardianv2 = false
guardian_ext = false
apps = false
enable_mcp_apps = false

plugin_sharing = false
recommended_plugins = false

Next, configure the config.toml file. config.toml tells the ChatGPT desktop app how to operate, including which model provider to use (amazon-bedrock), which model to select, and settings such as permissions or context limits.

Replace the model ID and named profile (for example, codex-il5) with approved values.

model = "REPLACE_WITH_APPROVED_MODEL_ID"
model_provider = "amazon-bedrock"
forced_login_method = "api"
approval_policy = { granular = { sandbox_approval = false,
rules = true, mcp_elicitations = false,
request_permissions = false, skill_approval = true } }
approvals_reviewer = "user"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
web_search = "cached"

check_for_update_on_startup = false

wire_api = "responses"

supports_websockets = false
supports_standalone_web_search = false

[model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws]
region = "us-gov-west-1"
profile = "codex-il5"

[sandbox_workspace_write]

[analytics]
enabled = false

enabled = false

[otel]

trace_exporter = "none"

[memories]
generate_memories = false
use_memories = false

[skills.bundled]
enabled = false

[apps._default]
enabled = false

[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"

Step 3: Launch, initialize, and verify

Download the app from the ChatGPT site and install it. Leave the app closed after installation. If it opens automatically or if the app has been launched previously, fully exit ChatGPT and end any lingering ChatGPT or Codex processes.

Make sure requirements.toml and config.toml are in place before the first app launch.

Start the app to load the requirements.toml and config.toml settings. Make sure it shows amazon-bedrock as the model provider.

In the Codex CLI, you should see a /status tab that looks like this:

Figure 1: The Codex CLI /status tab confirming amazon-bedrock as the model provider

In the ChatGPT desktop app, you can also confirm amazon-bedrock as the model provider.

Figure 2: The ChatGPT desktop app settings showing amazon-bedrock as the model provider

Troubleshooting

The application prompts for an OpenAI account. Verify that requirements.toml and config.toml use the exact locations and file names shown in the preceding table, terminate all ChatGPT and Codex processes, and relaunch. The files must precede app launch.

AWS GovCloud (US) endpoint is reported as unsupported. Confirm the exact desktop or app-server release, endpoint, and model with OpenAI. Changing the URL alone does not establish support.

The wrong AWS identity is used. Inspect the effective credential source and named profile. Check whether an Amazon Bedrock API key takes precedence over the profile.

Capability restrictions are missing. Inspect the full effective requirements after restart. The API-only sign-in setting doesn’t apply the capability policy.

Rollback and cleanup

If a validation check fails, stop the rollout. Return the affected devices to the previously approved policy and provider settings, then restart the ChatGPT desktop app. Revoke any temporary AWS credentials or API keys, and confirm that those devices can no longer connect to Amazon Bedrock. Keep a record of the test and clearly document what failed before trying again.

Conclusion

The ChatGPT desktop app on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) gives you a controlled way to use OpenAI frontier models and coding assistance. Inference stays in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. By validating the configuration, confirming the approved AWS identity and endpoint, and verifying security controls, you can confidently prepare the deployment for broader use. This approach supports innovation while aligning deployment decisions with each organization’s security, authorization, and data-handling requirements.

Ready to explore the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)? Start with a controlled deployment, validate your security controls, and work with your security team to prepare for broader adoption.

item.title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
item.dc:creator: Priyanka Bettaswamygowda
item.description: The UK Amazon Quick User Group's 2026 roundup: three quarterly meetups, 150+ attendees, and customer stories from Arriva, Carsa, and Propulse Lab on using agentic AI and Amazon Quick to turn data into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth.
item.content:encoded:
The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together.

Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI.

Why Amazon Quick user groups matter

The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can:

  • Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. Members share what works, what doesn’t, and new approaches that drive results.
  • Network – Connect with regional professionals who are solving similar use cases with Amazon Quick for enterprise AI applications, data analytics, and workplace productivity.
  • Problem-solve – Tackle challenges collaboratively by discussing solutions and use cases across different industries and business contexts.
  • Stay updated – Get firsthand knowledge about new features, updates, and emerging best practices directly from peers and experts.
  • Build community – Foster a local support network that complements the broader Amazon Quick community, with trusted contacts who understand UK market and business context.

Event overview

Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate, while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper.

What a typical event looks like

All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins.

From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback session, the room feels more like a working group than an audience.

The format has shifted each quarter. Q1 leaned more on introductions and demos because the group was meeting for the first time. By Q2, we added an icebreaker quiz, and ran a focused workshop on Quick Flows and automation. For Q3 we brought in a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a networking slot at the end. That last one came about because people were already staying behind to talk after the close, so we stopped packing up around them and put it in the schedule.

Figure 1: Attendees at a UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup

What customers shared

Customer stories have been part of the community from the start. Each speaker brought a different problem into the room, showing how teams are applying Quick in very different environments.

At the first event, the conversation centered on getting insight into the hands of the people who need it. At Arriva UK Trains, critical data wasn’t reaching the people who needed it most. Train and station managers were constantly on the move, relying solely on their work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and introduced pixel perfect reports automatically delivered through scheduled email, giving managers immediate visibility of incidents and performance. The result: faster decisions, better incident management, and a stronger data-driven culture across the organization.

By Q2, the discussion had moved toward a different challenge: getting the foundations right before introducing more AI and automation. At Carsa, a used-car retailer, analytics functioned like a service desk. Question in, dashboard out. The same question gave different answers. It wasn’t a data problem. It was a definitions problem. Tobi Daramola’s team at Carsa fixed this by building a single governed data layer, with metrics defined once and consumed by Amazon Quick and AI assistants alike. As a result, they removed 50 percent of dashboards while surfacing more data. Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores moved 10 percent in 30 days, complaints same-day close rate jumped 20 percent, and AI on the layer cut recurring tasks from 45 minutes to 5.

Q3 brought the conversation further into automation and agentic workflows. Propulse Lab, a Swiss operating system for B2C subscription businesses, was handling 1 million support tickets a year. Their teams were stuck firefighting instead of driving growth. After deploying a multi-agent AI pipeline in Amazon Quick Automate, built from their best past customer service interactions, they cut request handling from 7 minutes to 70 seconds. The pipeline also automated 80 percent of routine workflows.

“What was once a cost centre became a growth engine – their product managers now own the entire system without writing a single line of code, and their support teams focus on proactive, revenue-driving conversations instead.”

— Guirec Lecointre, Growth Operations Specialist, Propulse Lab

The use cases vary widely, and that’s exactly the point. Rather than presenting a single vision for Amazon Quick, practitioners show what they’ve tried against real business problems, from governed analytics and frontline reporting to automation and AI. That shifts the conversation in the room. Attendees ask direct questions about implementation, adoption, and what didn’t work. Speakers share the practical lessons behind the finished solution. People leave with ideas they can apply to their own organizations, not just another customer story.

From presentations to participation

Attendees changed across the three events. A listen-and-learn turned into building meaningful relationships by Q3. People were new to the group and new to each other. By Q2, the icebreaker quiz loosened things up early. The feedback sessions got more specific too: instead of “this was great,” people were requesting topics and offering to contribute.

Q3 pushes this further. Sofia Bourika, who joined the leadership team early on and presented the Arriva customer story at the first event, came up with an icebreaker called “What Are You Proud Of?”, attendees share something they’ve built with Amazon Quick. We’ve already got someone who was previously sitting in the audience volunteering to present their work. That kind of shift, from attending to contributing, took three events to happen, but it happened. Q3 also introduced a new segment, the Amazon Quick specialist panel. Questions were pre-collected from the audience and posed to an invited specialist, who brought real depth to the answers and shared first-hand experience of working with attendees’ customers. It sparked a different kind of thinking in the room, with the audience connecting the dots between the specialist’s insights and their own day-to-day challenges.

Our community stayed connected all year. Our LinkedIn group had weekly contributions and our email lists encouraged involvement.

Collective impact in action

A huge thank you to our dedicated AWS Partner, Data Reply, whose consistent contributions and thought leadership have been instrumental in making every UK user group meetup a success.

Our UK leadership team led us to reach every milestone:

Liam Yusuph, AI and Data Delivery Lead, Data Reply

Priyanka Bettaswamygowda, Solutions Architect, AWS

Sahar Shahbaz, Data Analyst, Data Reply

Sofia Bourika, Lead BI Developer, Arriva

Tobi Daramola, Senior Data and Analytics Lead, Carsa

Ali Hayat, AV Support Associate, Amazon

Lam Phan, BI Developer, AWS

Rikhi Singh, ADC Engineer, AWS

Figure 2: The UK Amazon Quick User Group leadership team

Amazon Quick Community resources

The Amazon Quick Community website has tens of thousands of members and thousands of searchable questions. It also offers over 600 learning resources on accelerating your productivity with agentic AI and Amazon Quick.

“The Quick Community is about learning together and building connections. It’s where users at any skill level can find help, learn something new, and meet others. What I love most about the Quick Community is how genuinely helpful everyone is. It’s a place that reveals possibilities you wouldn’t have thought to explore on your own, where you stumble into people working on projects and use cases, you’d never even think to ask about, and suddenly your world gets a whole lot bigger.”

— Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, AWS

Learning opportunities include approximately two free live online sessions per week, monthly feature update detailed and advanced automation sessions, and 4-hour Immersion Day workshops. AWS Solutions Architects, Product Managers, and subject matter experts are active on the platform and available for direct messaging. Kristin continues, “People jump in to help solve tricky problems, share their clever workarounds, and experiment with new ways to use Quick together.”

Key takeaways

A few themes came up consistently across the three events.

The format keeps changing because we listen

The Amazon Quick User Group UK runs on a set structure: an introduction, a product update, customer stories, a hands-on workshop, and a feedback session. But we’ve been adjusting it every quarter. Early on, we had the “What’s New with Quick” segment right after customer stories, and it broke the flow. People were engaged with how a real company was using the product, then we’d switch to feature announcements. We moved “What’s New” so the customer stories lead straight into the workshop, and the difference was noticeable. For Q3, we added an interactive quiz to get more back-and-forth going in the room. Attendees also called out the overall format and pacing, and the chance to meet new people. As one first-time attendee put it, “the networking opportunities were excellent… I thoroughly enjoyed the day!”.

Customers present, not us

At least one customer shares how they use Amazon Quick at each event. Across three events, we’ve had Carsa, Arriva, Propulse Lab, and a few other customers on stage. After the very first event, one of the clearest pieces of feedback was that people wanted more customer speakers. That told us we were on the right track. The sessions work because the audience is hearing from peers who face similar problems, not from someone trying to sell them something. The impact goes beyond the event itself. Attendees said the customer stories showed them new ways to use the tools and started useful discussions about return on investment (ROI). One attendee told us a customer session “has already prompted a lot of conversation internally” at their organization.

The workshop is where it clicks

Every event has a hands-on workshop, and people consistently tell us it’s the part they get the most out of. There’s a gap between watching someone demo a product and sitting down with it yourself. That gap is where most attendees say Amazon Quick starts to make sense for what they’re trying to do. We know it lands because the most common question afterwards is whether they can keep access to the workshop environment so they can carry on experimenting on their own.

Conclusion

The success of this year’s meetups is a testament to every single member who showed up, shared their knowledge, and contributed to making this community what it is today. As we look ahead, we’re more energized than ever to keep this momentum going and continue pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with Amazon Quick.

Get involved

To learn more about Amazon Quick and connect with the community:

  • Join the UK Amazon Quick User Group on LinkedIn.
  • Join the Amazon Quick Community to learn agentic AI together and access over 600 learning resources.
  • Explore Amazon Bedrock for additional generative AI capabilities.
  • Register for the next UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup: January 28, 2027.
  • Not in the UK? Attend a meetup in Austin, Phoenix, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles, New York City, or Munich/DACH.
  • Complete the leadership interest form to start an Amazon Quick User Group in your city.

For questions about the event or the Amazon Quick Community, Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, Amazon Quick Community and User Group program, at kmandia@amazon.com.

 

About the authors

Priyanka Bettaswamygowda

Priyanka is a Solutions Architect at AWS and has a great passion for Amazon Quick. Priyanka works with customers across the UK regional public sector to help adopt cloud technologies and accelerate innovation.

Liam Yusuph

Liam is an AI & Data Delivery Lead at Data Reply with a passion for AI-powered analytics and Amazon Quick. Liam leads the delivery of AI and data solutions, helping organizations turn emerging technologies into practical business value.

item.title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
item.dc:creator: Sakthi Chellapparimanam
item.description: Epsilon's Agentic Platform team delivers UI testing as a managed, multi-tenant service built on Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Tests are written in plain English and run on browsers managed by AWS, giving every product team resilient, intent-driven testing with zero per-team infrastructure overhead.
item.content:encoded:
To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon, a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe, turned to Amazon Nova Act. With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team.

Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own.

One of those managed capabilities is UI testing. With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform.

In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results.

The challenge: Enhancing coverage, not replacing what works

Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today.

The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective:

  • Scripted Playwright tests are effective for deterministic regression checks. However, they are tightly coupled to selectors and page structure. Cosmetic UI changes can break them even when the underlying functionality is sound.
  • Multiple product teams needed full testing coverage against their own applications. Standing up browser infrastructure, managing dependencies, and integrating with identity systems per team created duplicative effort.
  • The platform team wanted UI testing to be a managed capability that fit their existing agent model, not a custom CLI that every onboarded team had to operate.

The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability.

Why Epsilon chose Amazon Nova Act and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool

Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both.

  • Natural-language steps. Test steps are plain-English instructions executed by Nova Act. They are resilient to cosmetic UI changes and readable by non-engineers. A step like “Confirm the rewards balance is visible” ages far better than a brittle CSS selector.
  • AWS managed, ephemeral browser sessions. With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get isolated browser instances with no binaries to ship and no display server to maintain. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool also offers live view for human observation or takeover (useful for CAPTCHAs or multi-factor authentication), session recording to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and AWS CloudTrail audit, all without additional configuration.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM)-based authentication. With Nova Act, you can authenticate through the standard AWS credential chain (the task role). This fits Epsilon’s existing security model without distributing separate API keys.
  • Cross-account friendly. With Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, you can slot into your existing AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) AssumeRole provisioning. Each onboarded team can run tests inside their own AWS account under a scoped role. This maintains isolation and auditability.

Epsilon chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool specifically because it eliminates the operational burden of managing browser binaries, display servers, and session lifecycle. The Agentic Platform team had no interest in owning that infrastructure.

The solution: Architecture and implementation

Epsilon’s solution has three main components: a platform API for creating workflows, a background task runner for executing them, and the Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration that drives the browser.

Platform architecture

Epsilon’s UI testing capability follows a clear pipeline:

  1. A user creates a workflow through the platform API, specifying a target_url and a list of natural-language steps.
  2. On create, the platform registers a Nova Act workflow definition on AWS.
  3. On execute, a background task runner (Celery, a Python framework for asynchronous job processing) opens an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool browser session. It runs each step through Nova Act over a Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) WebSocket (the standard interface for programmatically controlling Chromium browsers), including conditional logic (for example, “if a tour box appears, skip it”).
  4. The system captures a screenshot per step, tracks pass/fail per step, computes an overall pass rate, and stores everything (results JSON, screenshots in Amazon S3, session ID).
  5. A completion hook fires so the result is recorded back into the platform.

Figure 1: Epsilon’s UI Testing Service architecture

Figure 1 shows the layered architecture of Epsilon’s UI Testing Service. User requests flow from the Agent Cloud Frontend through an API Gateway with authentication and permission checks. The API layer (Django REST) exposes endpoints for workflows, executions, automation suites, and stats. The business logic layer includes a Workflow Manager, Execution Orchestrator, and Suite Coordinator. Test jobs are queued in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and picked up by the Runner Service running on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), which contains the Nova Act engine and a headless Chromium browser. Results, screenshots, trajectories, and HTML reports are stored in Amazon S3.

The capability is exposed as a standard agent (ui-test-agent) with two skills:

  • ui-test-recorder: Explore a scenario interactively and record natural-language steps.
  • ui-test-executor: Run recorded steps and return structured results.

Onboarded teams consume UI testing the same way they consume any other platform agent. No additional infrastructure to manage. The onboarding process is straightforward. The platform team provisions a cross-account IAM role for the new team, registers their target application URLs, and grants access to the ui-test-agent through the existing platform API. From that point, teams create workflows, trigger executions, and retrieve results through the same interface they already use for other platform capabilities.

The core integration

The Nova Act + Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration is concise:

import boto3
from bedrock_agentcore.tools.browser_client import browser_session
from nova_act import NovaAct

boto_session = boto3.Session(region_name=region)

with browser_session(region) as client:
    ws_url, headers = client.generate_ws_headers()
    with NovaAct(
        cdp_endpoint_url=ws_url,
        cdp_headers=headers,
        boto_session=boto_session,
        starting_page=url
    ) as nova_act:
        result = nova_act.act(instruction)

This pattern (open a managed browser session, connect through the CDP WebSocket, and drive actions with natural language) is the foundation. Epsilon wraps it with their platform’s multi-tenant orchestration, result capture, and observability layers.

Example: Automating the ‘Create an agent’ flow

To illustrate intent-based testing, here is a representative workflow from Epsilon’s platform. It exercises login, form entry, conditional handling, scrolling, and verification. The following steps highlight the differentiating patterns of Nova Act:

Step Instruction
1 Type the username and choose Next
2 Enter the password and choose Verify
3 Navigate to Create Agent and select the Design a new specification card
4 If an onboarding tour box appears, choose Skip Tour, then verify the correct page loaded
5 Fill in the agent name and description fields
6 Scroll down until the Goal Statement field is visible, then fill it in
7 If the skills search box is not visible, scroll until it appears. Then search for and add a skill
8 Choose Save, confirm the success prompt, navigate back, and verify the new agent appears in the list

Steps 4 and 7 demonstrate conditional logic: “if an element appears, handle it” and “if a target isn’t visible, scroll until it is.” These patterns would require explicit branching in a traditional framework. Nova Act handles them naturally through language understanding.

Runtime isolation

Epsilon runs UI tests in a dedicated runner service (a FastAPI sidecar) that pins nova-act 3.x with Workflow and IAM authentication support, plus the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool client. This keeps dependencies separate from the main backend so they don’t collide with the Strands agent stack. The worker falls back to in-process execution if the runner is disabled, providing resilience during deployments.

Best practices

Based on their experience building UI testing as a platform capability, the Epsilon team recommends:

1. Write steps as intent, not mechanics

GOOD: "Confirm the rewards balance is visible"
BAD: await page.locator('#rewards-balance-container > span.amount').toBeVisible()

Intent-based steps survive UI redesigns. Product managers and quality assurance (QA) leads who might not write code can review them directly.

2. Isolate the Nova Act runtime

Pin Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool dependencies in a dedicated service or container. Epsilon learned that the signing endpoint for Nova Act targets us-east-1 regardless of the browser session’s region. Running it in a separate service with its own dependency lockfile prevents hard-to-debug conflicts.

3. Reuse recorded trajectories to cut cost

Epsilon uses trajectory retries in draft state, saves the successful trajectory, and replays it in active state. Repeat runs skip redundant large language model (LLM) “thinking,” reducing both latency and cost for regression-style repeated executions.

4. Design for multi-tenancy from day one

Use cross-account AssumeRole with scoped IAM policies. Each tenant’s tests run under their own role in their own account. This provides isolation, auditability, and failure scope containment without custom infrastructure per team.

5. Lean on managed observability

With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get live view, session recording, and AWS CloudTrail integration. Epsilon uses these built-in capabilities instead of building custom observability, reducing maintenance and giving compliance teams familiar audit surfaces.

6. Account for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool viewport behavior

When prompting Nova Act steps, account for the browser viewport defaults of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Steps that reference scrolling (for example, “scroll down until the Goal Statement textbox is visible”) verify that Nova Act handles content in the lower portion of the page correctly.

Results and impact

Epsilon’s UI testing capability is operational across multiple teams, with the multi-tenant architecture proven in production.

Dimension Amazon Nova Act Playwright (equivalent)
Lines authored 18 natural-language steps ~80-150 lines of code
Selector/DOM inspection None Required per interactive step
Authoring time (per workflow) ~5-10 minutes ~30-90 minutes
Effort ratio Baseline 4-6x more effort

Here are the measured outcomes:

  • 4-6x faster test authoring (based on Epsilon’s internal benchmarks). A representative 18-step workflow took 5–10 minutes to author with Nova Act, compared to 30–90 minutes for the equivalent Playwright script (80–150 lines of code). Each interactive step in the Playwright script requires inspecting the DOM, choosing a stable selector, and coding explicit waits, assertions, and branching for conditional cases. Nova Act replaces that per-step overhead with 18 natural-language instructions and zero selector or DOM inspection, with conditional logic (such as the tour-box and scroll-until-visible steps) expressed in plain English.
  • 100 percent pass rate on trajectory replay (based on Epsilon’s internal benchmarks). After a workflow passes the initial explore phase (typically 4–5 prompt iterations), Epsilon saves the successful trajectory and replays it deterministically. Saved trajectories achieve a 100 percent pass rate across repeated runs.
  • Lower barrier to test authoring. Steps read like plain English. Team members beyond core test engineers can read, review, and propose tests, broadening ownership of quality.
  • Built-in audit trail. AWS CloudTrail integration and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool session recording made debugging and compliance conversations easier. This was a benefit the team did not initially set out to achieve.
  • Zero per-team infrastructure overhead. Onboarded teams get UI testing through the same API surface as every other platform agent. No browser binaries, no Selenium grid, no display servers to manage.
  • Pass/fail visibility per step. Screenshot capture at each step provides granular debugging context, reducing mean time to diagnose failures.

“Nova Act let us turn UI testing from a brittle, selector-chasing chore into a managed platform capability. Our tests now describe intent in plain English, run on AWS managed browsers, and every product team we onboard gets reliable testing without additional configuration.”

— Epsilon Agentic Platform Team

Learn more

Epsilon’s Agentic Platform team demonstrated how to deliver resilient, intent-driven UI testing as a managed service using Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. You can apply the same pattern to your own multi-tenant platform to eliminate browser infrastructure overhead and make test authoring accessible to non-engineers.

If you want to build similar intent-driven UI testing capabilities with Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, here are resources to get started:

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool User Guide
  • Nova Act Python SDK on PyPI
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Documentation
  • Nova Act + Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool sample code (GitHub)
  • Related post: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act

To learn more about how your organization can use intent-based browser automation for testing, visit the Amazon Nova Act product page.
