item.title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
item.dc:creator: Sarat Guttikonda
item.description: Turn a PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process with Kiro. This post walks through a reusable engine: a mechanical discovery scanner and an eight-phase, parity-first workflow that treats the original PHP application as the specification and verifies the Java port with a parity harness.
item.content:encoded:
When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently.

This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro. Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it.

Prerequisites

Before getting started, you need:

  • Familiarity with PHP (Laravel/Eloquent or Symfony/Doctrine). Java knowledge (Spring Boot, JPA) helps you review the generated output, but the engine produces idiomatic Java for you, so you don’t need to rewrite the application in Java yourself.
  • A Kiro workspace with access to Skills and Steering files.
  • PHP 8.0 or newer on the machine running the discovery scanner, and Java 21 with Maven for the generated Spring Boot projects.
  • A basic understanding of migration planning (discovery, translation, and validation).

What you will learn in this post

You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way.

Two ways to run the engine: Kiro and AWS Transform

Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways.

Method 1: Kiro, interactive and developer-in-the-loop

Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post.

Method 2: AWS Transform, agentic and at portfolio scale

AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘fix the loop, not the code’ apply to an autonomous run.

When each path fits

  • Control and autonomy: Use Kiro to work through the code first: run the skill on one application, read the generated Java, and run the tests. When you want to migrate more, AWS Transform runs the same methodology agentically with review at the checkpoints the skill defines.
  • Scale and novelty: Kiro handles one application at a time and suits first-of-a-kind frameworks. AWS Transform runs many applications as parallel jobs.
  • A shared feedback loop: Both paths read the same skill files, so every rulebook fix made in Kiro improves the next AWS Transform run, and vice versa.

Solution overview: One shared brain, many projects

The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. To open it, clone the repository locally, then in Kiro open a folder and select the repository root (the folder containing .kiro/). Kiro loads the skills and steering automatically, with fuller steps in “Getting started.”

The workspace separates a shared methodology layer from the individual projects that use it, as shown in the following diagram. At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on. Beneath it sit the per-project folders, each with its own PHP source, Java output, and specification sub-folder.

Figure 1: The workspace is split into a shared, global methodology layer and per-project code and spec folders

Those same shared skill files can be run in two different ways, shown in the following diagram. The identical eight-phase, parity-first pipeline can be driven either by Kiro (interactive, one application at a time) or by AWS Transform (agentic, at portfolio scale), and both convert PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java.

Figure 2: The same shared skill files drive two execution paths: Kiro (interactive, one app at a time) and AWS Transform (agentic, portfolio scale). Both run the identical eight-phase parity-first pipeline, converting PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java

A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight-phase playbook), plus the core-workflow.md Steering file. Each per-project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub-folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain.

Discovery before translation

The single most important rule fires before anything else: Don’t read, guess at, or hand-translate a model or entity file until the scanner has run.

The scanner works in a single pass with no dependencies, as shown in the following diagram. It applies three discovery strategies to the source tokens and emits one JSON manifest, with anything ambiguous routed to a review-flag queue for a human to resolve.

Figure 3: The scanner runs three discovery strategies over source tokens and emits a single JSON manifest with a review-flag queue

The scanner is discover-models.php, a single-file, dependency-free PHP command-line tool that doesn’t execute the target code. It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed. It runs three strategies on every scan: Eloquent model discovery (walking the class inheritance chain to Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model), Doctrine attribute detection (the #[ORM\Entity] attribute), and ORM XML mapping (external *.orm.xml files). The output is a single JSON manifest. A models[] array carries every field, cast, relationship, and visibility rule, and a flags[] array appears on every entry. The scanner flags ambiguity rather than guessing. For example, a $fillable list built from a runtime expression becomes a plain-English flag, and that flag list is the human review queue.

The parity-first pipeline

Phase 0 is preparatory: it runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. The first three phases then concentrate human expertise. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application.

Figure 4: Human judgment is front-loaded into a preparatory Phase 0 and Phases 1–3. Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops, refereed by a parity harness

The first four phases concentrate human expertise. Phase 0 runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application.

Phase Name Deliverable
0 Assess and discover Model manifest + inventory + cutover choice
1 Build the judge Parity harness runnable against PHP and Java
2 Rulebook + gap inventory RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md
3 Stress-test the rulebook Hardened rulebook, validated against representative files
4 Scaffold Compiling Spring Boot project
5 Translate the data model JPA entities + schema baseline
6 Translate the I/O layer Controllers, security, templates respond
7 Convert business logic Logic converted, tests green
8 Prove parity and cut over Parity report + cutover checklist

Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops: Phase 4 scaffolds the project, Phase 5 translates the data model from the manifest, Phase 6 translates the I/O layer (routes become controllers, middleware becomes filters, validation becomes annotated data transfer objects), Phase 7 converts business logic in batches, and Phase 8 proves parity against the harness and cuts over. Two principles govern the loop. First, the PHP code is the specification: the port is done when the referee agrees, or each mismatch is logged as an approved change. Second, you fix the loop, not the code, amending the rulebook and regenerating rather than hand-patching.

Walkthrough: From Eloquent to Spring Boot

The laravel-eloquent-sample project is a working, bounded example: a read-only slice of an open source Laravel application, with the Book, Chapter, Page, and User models migrated to Spring Boot 3.4.1 on Java 21 with Maven and an in-memory H2 database.

The mapping from PHP to Spring Boot is mechanical and traceable, as shown in the following diagram. Each manifest entry on the left maps to a Java construct on the right, producing the layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice.

Figure 5: Manifest-driven mappings on the left. The layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice on the right

The mappings are mechanical and traceable back to the manifest: a PHP namespace becomes a Java package, an Eloquent model becomes a JPA @Entity, has Many and belongs to relationships become @OneToMany and @ManyToOne, and Eloquent query scopes become Spring Data repository methods. The discipline shows in serialization: html, markdown, and text carry @JsonIgnore because the manifest recorded them in Page’s $hidden list, while Book’s description deliberately doesn’t.

The spec is candid that only 4 of 37 models were ported and, most important, that the parity harness was never built for this slice, which it calls “the single biggest gap.” Documenting where it falls short is itself part of the design.

Getting started

The complete migration engine is available in the sample PHP-to-Java migration repository.

To use it:

  1. Clone the repository and open its root as your Kiro workspace (open a folder and select the folder containing .kiro/). Nothing to install beyond PHP 8.0+ for the scanner and Java 21 with Maven.
  2. Fetch the PHP source into the project’s source-php/ folder. The README pins the exact upstream commits used for parity so anyone can reproduce the baseline.
  3. Ask Kiro to migrate the application. The php-to-java-migration skill activates automatically, runs the scanner first, generates a fresh spec under .kiro/specs/, and walks you through the approval gates.
  4. For an agentic run, point AWS Transform at the same skill files, so its agents execute the identical methodology across your portfolio.

The methodology auto-detects Laravel, Symfony, CodeIgniter, and plain PHP, and extension is additive: add a detection row and a references/<framework>-to-spring.md guide for a new framework. Because Kiro and AWS Transform read the same files, refining them once upgrades both engines.

 

Clean up

If you deployed the sample Spring Boot application during this walkthrough:

  1. Stop the running Spring Boot application (the in-memory H2 database is ephemeral and requires no separate cleanup).
  2. Remove the generated Java project folder from your workspace if no longer needed.
  3. The discovery scanner produces only a JSON manifest file. Delete the discovery scanner’s JSON manifest from your working directory if you don’t plan to reference it.
  4. No AWS resources are provisioned by the migration engine itself, so there are no cloud resources to deprovision.

 

Conclusion

We showed how to build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro that turns large-scale rewrites into a measurable, compounding process. The key principles are:

  • Discovery before translation: A mechanical scanner inventories every model, field, and relationship, so you don’t guess at structure.
  • Build the judge before the code: A parity harness defines done before the first line of Java is written.
  • Fix the loop, not the code: When the same mistake appears across files, amend the rulebook and regenerate rather than hand-patching.
  • One shared brain: The methodology is written once, shared across projects, and improves with each migration.

None of this is specific to PHP or Java. The same shape applies to other migrations where the old system is the only complete specification. Clone the sample PHP-to-Java migration repository, open it as a Kiro workspace, and explore the Skills and Steering capabilities that power it, or bring the same skill files to AWS Transform. For more about language migration patterns on AWS, see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance documentation.

item.title: Lend and borrow resources across teams with AWS Batch’s quota management for SageMaker Training jobs
item.dc:creator: Michelle Goodstein
item.description: AWS Batch quota management is a new scheduling capability you can use to divide GPU capacity into quota shares per team or project, automatically lend idle capacity across shares, and use preemption to run your highest-priority SageMaker Training jobs first, all without manual coordination.
item.content:encoded:
With the launch of AWS Batch support for Amazon SageMaker Training jobs, customers gained a new fully managed way to queue, schedule, and retry machine learning (ML) training workloads without building their own infrastructure. Instead, they use the queuing and scheduling features of AWS Batch. As organizations scale their artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) operations and onboard more teams, coordinating access to shared graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity can introduce additional communication, coordination, and configuration overhead for administrators. This overhead includes setting up separate queues, adjusting capacity limits, and carefully orchestrating the right workloads to get the right resources at the right time. A core value proposition of AWS Batch is helping customers increase utilization of their compute, and as training environments grow, so does the opportunity to do more with existing capacity.

Working backward from customers managing multi-team training environments, we heard a consistent request: give us a way to define allocations per team or project, share idle capacity automatically, and run our highest-priority workloads first. This request led us to build quota management, a new scheduling capability for AWS Batch. Administrators can use it to divide compute capacity into quota shares, organized by team, project, or workload. Each quota share uses configurable resource-sharing strategies that maximize GPU utilization while honoring each team’s allocation when it matters most.

This post shows how quota management works, including how to configure quota shares with lending and borrowing strategies, set up in-share preemption for priority workloads, and get started using the SageMaker Python SDK.

Quota shares and preemption

Administrators can allocate and share constrained GPU resources by defining a quota share for separate entities, such as individual teams or projects. Each quota share includes compute quotas (capacity limits) and resource-sharing strategies for idle compute. These strategies determine whether idle compute is reserved until jobs arrive (RESERVE), lent to other quota shares that have work available (LEND), or both lent when idle and borrowed when the share has work that might benefit (LEND_AND_BORROW).

A quota share operates as a virtual queue nested hierarchically within an associated job queue. When scheduling jobs for a job queue, AWS Batch prioritizes quota shares that are under their capacity limits as it iterates through the associated quota shares. If jobs arrive in a quota share that has lent out its capacity, AWS Batch performs cross-share preemption. This reclaims resources for the lending quota share, so administrators don’t need to track down the jobs borrowing capacity and terminate them on their own. If jobs arrive in a quota share that is at or above its capacity limit, AWS Batch checks whether there’s available capacity to borrow from another quota share. If so, workloads can run using otherwise-idle capacity.

You can turn on priority-based in-share preemption when you configure a quota share. Where cross-share preemption reclaims lent capacity as jobs arrive in a lending quota share, in-share preemption preempts lower priority jobs that are in the SCHEDULED, STARTING, or RUNNING state. This allows higher priority jobs at the front of the queue to start running sooner.

Prerequisites

Before you proceed with this example, you must have an AWS account with permissions to create and manage AWS Batch resources. For this example, see the sample IAM permissions needed to invoke AWS Batch and SageMaker APIs.

The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3. Complete the setup required to install a compatible version of the SageMaker Python SDK:

!pip install sagemaker

Configuring quota management resources

Using the new quota management capabilities requires creating a Scheduling Policy that contains a quotaSharePolicy, a Service Environment that specifies its capacity limits in terms of specific instances, and a SageMaker Training job queue that is connected to both. After that, you can associate quota shares to a job queue. The user guide has AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and console examples for configuring quota management resources and quota shares. An end-to-end example of quota management integrated with the aws_batch module in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 is contained in a sample notebook. In this example, we step through code snippets that summarize the key components, and use the helper functions from the notebook to create a Scheduling Policy, Service Environment, Job Queue, and three Quota Shares.

The three quota shares configured here represent three different projects. Each has the same capacity limit set: a single ml.g5.xlarge instance. The QS1 quota share represents background jobs. For this project, you want to run the most important background job first and borrow as much spare capacity as is available. Within this quota share, no jobs are urgent, and preemptions are acceptable because all jobs use checkpointing. This quota share uses the LEND_AND_BORROW resource-sharing strategy and has in-share preemption turned on. Higher priority jobs within the same quota share can then preempt running jobs that are lower priority.

from sagemaker.train.aws_batch.boto_client import get_batch_boto_client
from utils.aws_batch_resource_management import AwsBatchResourceManager, QuotaShareConfig, create_quota_management_resources

INSTANCE_TYPE = "ml.g5.xlarge"

# Create SchedulingPolicy, ServiceEnvironment, JobQueue, and QuotaShares
resource_manager = AwsBatchResourceManager(get_batch_boto_client())
qs1 = QuotaShareConfig(
    name="QS1",
    capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE,
    max_capacity=1,
    in_share_preemption=True,
    sharing_strategy="LEND_AND_BORROW",
    borrow_limit=200
)

QS2 represents medium priority workloads. Teams choosing this configuration would prefer to wait for capacity to become available rather than endure additional preemptions. Those preemptions come from borrowed capacity being reclaimed or from in-share preemptions because of higher priority job submission. This is appropriate for shorter jobs, or when most submitted jobs have similar priorities. The quota share still benefits from job priority being taken into consideration at job dispatch. Submitted jobs trigger AWS Batch to reclaim any lent capacity needed to run the jobs.

qs2 = QuotaShareConfig(
    name="QS2",
    capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE,
    max_capacity=1,
    in_share_preemption=False,
    sharing_strategy="LEND"
)

QS3 represents workloads that need to start as quickly as possible with minimal interruptions. It’s configured to reserve capacity and neither lends nor borrows to other quota shares. It doesn’t experience cross-share preemptions, because its workloads don’t exceed their capacity limits. By also turning off in-share preemption, workloads submitted to this quota share are not preempted by AWS Batch as long as the capacity limit is unchanged.

qs3 = QuotaShareConfig(
    name="QS3",
    capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE,
    max_capacity=1,
    in_share_preemption=False,
    sharing_strategy="RESERVE"
)

These quota share configurations are inputs to the create_quota_management_resources function in the sample notebook, which also configures the corresponding Scheduling Policy, Service Environment, and Job Queue with the constant names chosen.

SCHEDULING_POLICY_NAME = "my-qm-scheduling-policy"
JOB_QUEUE_NAME = "my-sm-training-qm-jq"
SERVICE_ENVIRONMENT_NAME = "my-sm-training-qm-se"

resources = create_quota_management_resources(
    resource_manager=resource_manager,
    scheduling_policy_name=SCHEDULING_POLICY_NAME,
    job_queue_name=JOB_QUEUE_NAME,
    service_environment_name=SERVICE_ENVIRONMENT_NAME,
    capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE,
    max_capacity=3,
    quota_share_configs=[qs1, qs2, qs3]
)

Submit SageMaker Training jobs to QS1

The aws_batch module within the SageMaker Python SDK has been extended to allow programmatic submission of SageMaker Training jobs to a quota-management-enabled AWS Batch job queue. To demonstrate these new capabilities, we use a Hello World ModelTrainer that’s submitted to the job queue. The following code snippet identifies an image URI to use based on the Region and instance type selected.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
)
logging.getLogger("botocore.client").setLevel(level=logging.WARN)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

from sagemaker.core.helper.session_helper import Session
from sagemaker.core import image_uris

session = Session()

image_uri = image_uris.retrieve(
    framework="pytorch",
    region=session.boto_session.region_name,
    version="2.5",
    instance_type=INSTANCE_TYPE,
    image_scope="training",
)

We use this image URI within a basic hello world model trainer example:

from sagemaker.train.model_trainer import ModelTrainer
from sagemaker.train.configs import SourceCode, Compute, StoppingCondition

TRAINING_JOB_NAME = "hello-world-simple-job"
MAX_RUN_TIME = 300

source_code = SourceCode(command="echo 'Hello World'")

model_trainer = ModelTrainer(
    training_image=image_uri,
    source_code=source_code,
    base_job_name=TRAINING_JOB_NAME,
    compute=Compute(instance_type=INSTANCE_TYPE, instance_count=INSTANCE_COUNT),
    stopping_condition=StoppingCondition(max_runtime_in_seconds=MAX_RUN_TIME),
)

To use the job queue within the SageMaker Python SDK, provide the queue name to the TrainingQueue constructor within the aws_batch module.

from sagemaker.train.aws_batch.training_queue import TrainingQueue, TrainingQueuedJob

# Construct the queue object using the SageMaker Python SDK
queue = TrainingQueue(JOB_QUEUE_NAME)
logger.info(f"Using queue: {queue.queue_name}")

We can then submit three jobs to QS1, our background jobs quota share. The first job submitted has the highest priority, followed by the medium priority job, and then the lowest priority job. As nothing is currently running in QS1 or QS2, two instances’ worth of jobs should start, corresponding to the first and second jobs submitted (as they had the highest relative priority). Note that because this is only a hello world training job, it doesn’t require data, but typically a ModelTrainer requires data to perform training.

from utils.aws_batch_resource_management import JobStatus, await_jobs, list_jobs_by_quota_share

# Submit three jobs to QS1, all with different priorities to guarantee dispatch ordering.
qs1_job_high: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs1_job_high", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs1.name, priority=3, inputs=None)
qs1_job_med: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs1_job_med", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs1.name, priority=2, inputs=None)
qs1_job_low: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs1_job_low", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs1.name, priority=1, inputs=None)

logger.info(f"Submitted jobs: {qs1_job_high.job_name}, {qs1_job_med.job_name}, {qs1_job_low.job_name}")
logger.info(f"Waiting for jobs to transition...")

# qs1_job_high is dispatched first using capacity from QS1, and qs1_job_med is dispatched second borrowing idle capacity from QS2
await_jobs([([qs1_job_high, qs1_job_med], JobStatus.dispatched() | JobStatus.terminal())])
list_jobs_by_quota_share(queue, [qs1.name, qs2.name, qs3.name], JobStatus.active())

Submitting jobs to QS2 triggers cross-share preemption to reclaim lent capacity

The team that owns QS2 might discover they have work to perform and submit a job to QS2. Doing so triggers a preemption of capacity back from QS1, which is currently borrowing that capacity (QS3’s capacity isn’t configured to be borrowed). This is a cross-share preemption.

# When a job is submitted to QS2, it will preempt its capacity back from QS1
qs2_job_1: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs2_job_1", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs2.name, priority=1, inputs=None)

logger.info(f"Submitted job {qs2_job_1.job_name}")
logger.info(f"Waiting for jobs to transition...")

await_jobs([
    ([qs2_job_1], JobStatus.dispatched() | JobStatus.terminal()),
    ([qs1_job_med], {JobStatus.RUNNABLE}) # Lowest priority QS1 job will be preempted
])
list_jobs_by_quota_share(queue, [qs1.name, qs2.name, qs3.name], JobStatus.active())

Updating job priorities in QS1 triggers in-share preemption to run highest priority jobs

If a scientist realizes that the qs1_job_low job in QS1, which is still RUNNABLE, needs to begin running now because of changing priorities, they can use the new UpdateServiceJob API to increase the priority of an already submitted job in QS1. Because there’s no available capacity to borrow, this kicks off an in-share preemption, so that the job currently running is preempted and qs1_job_low can begin.

# Updating qs1_job_low to be the highest priority job in QS1
qs1_job_low.update(scheduling_priority=4)

logger.info(f"Updated job {qs1_job_low.job_name} to increase its priority")
logger.info(f"Waiting for jobs to transition...")

await_jobs([
    ([qs1_job_low], JobStatus.dispatched() | JobStatus.terminal()),
    ([qs1_job_high], {JobStatus.RUNNABLE}) # High priority job will preempt lower priority jobs within the same quota share
])
list_jobs_by_quota_share(queue, [qs1.name, qs2.name, qs3.name], JobStatus.active())

(Optional) Clean up created resources

To clean up the resources created in this post, run the following code:

from utils.aws_batch_resource_management import delete_resources

delete_resources(resource_manager, resources)

Conclusion

In this post, we covered quota management, a new scheduling capability in AWS Batch, and how to use it with SageMaker Training jobs and get started setting up quota shares for your own projects. For more details, see the AWS Batch quota management user guide.

AWS Batch with quota management can help your organization increase compute utilization and more effectively prioritize your teams and workloads, freeing up time for your infrastructure admins and ML scientists. By implementing quota management, your teams can focus on their workloads and reduce time spent managing and coordinating infrastructure. This capability is especially powerful with Amazon SageMaker AI training plans, so that your organization can reserve capacity in the quantity you need, during the time you need it. By using AWS Batch with SageMaker AI, you can make full use of the training plan. We encourage you to try out this new capability so it can make a meaningful impact in your operations.

While working on AWS Batch, she led scheduling improvements for AI/ML, including quota management for SageMaker Training jobs, to drive utilization, efficiency, and cost optimization, as well as improved observability into the job execution lifecycle. She enjoys building innovative solutions to distributed systems problems spanning data, compute, and AI/ML.

item.title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Kumar
item.description: MoEngage turned roughly 400 private REST APIs across 7 AWS Regions into permission-scoped agent tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. No per-service MCP servers, no public endpoints, and no 400-tool context bloat. See how OpenAPI specs, Cedar policies, and managed Amazon VPC Lattice egress made it work.
item.content:encoded:
This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage.

When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions.

MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part.

In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path.

Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it.

Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work.

So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec.

That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API.

Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better.

Four constraints that shaped the architecture

Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable.

Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. Every new API would mean another networking change request, another set of security reviews, another piece of infrastructure to maintain.

Identity can’t be an agent’s decision. Every internal API call carries tenant, user, role, and database context. If that context is a large language model (LLM)-visible tool parameter, a model can get it wrong or be talked into changing it. MoEngage needed identity to be structurally out of the model’s reach, injected by the calling service and not surfaced as something the model can set or override.

A 400-tool catalog doesn’t fit in a context window. At roughly 50 tokens of JSON schema per tool, a full tools/list across the estate is over 20,000 tokens transmitted on every connection. That token budget is spent before the agent does anything useful, and it crowds out the context the agent actually needs to reason about the task. Client-side filtering (tool_filter in ADK or the MCP SDK) doesn’t fix this. The full catalog has already crossed the wire, and filtering by client convention isn’t an authorization boundary. An agent that is not supposed to see write operations shouldn’t receive them in the first place.

That last constraint is the one that avoided the obvious alternatives. A custom central MCP server solves the 20-servers problem but still leaves MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, none of it making MoEngage’s product better.

How AgentCore Gateway maps to those constraints

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a fully managed MCP server. You register OpenAPI specs as targets and the gateway generates MCP tools from them, then routes calls to the backing services. Four properties mapped directly onto MoEngage’s constraints.

OpenAPI in, MCP tools out. There’s no MCP server to build or operate, and no separate artifact to keep in sync with the API. The spec teams already maintain is the tool definition. Each operation becomes a tool named Target___operationId, for example CampaignsAPI___searchCampaigns. When the spec changes, the tool changes. When a team adds an endpoint, the tool appears. When a team removes one, the tool disappears. No deployment, no protocol expertise, no coordination with the AI Platform team.

Cedar policies, evaluated before the catalog is serialized. The AgentCore policy engine uses partial evaluation to filter tools/list per principal. Each agent authenticates as its own IAM role, and its Cedar policy determines which tools it can see and call. This is what makes 400 tools tractable. It isn’t client-side filtering after the fact, but server-side scoping before the response is built.

A campaign QA bot, for example, gets read access to campaign and segment tools but can’t call a write operation:

permit(
    principal == Agent::"campaign-qa-bot-v1",
    action == Action::"tools/call",
    resource in ToolGroup::"campaigns-read"
);

forbid(
    principal == Agent::"campaign-qa-bot-v1",
    action == Action::"tools/call",
    resource in ToolGroup::"write-actions"
);

The bot doesn’t see write tools in its tools/list response. There’s nothing to filter on the client side because the tools weren’t sent.

Managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice. The gateway reaches MoEngage’s internal services through AgentCore managed egress rather than through networking MoEngage builds and operates. Inbound, the gateway is reachable only through a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public path to it. Onboarding a new API adds a target, not a network topology change. This is the property that broke the multiply by seven Regions problem. The networking exists once and every API uses it.

Semantic search as a gateway capability. With the x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search capability, an agent can find tools by describing the task instead of naming the tool. It removed the need for a custom discovery layer. It also removed rename fragility as a side effect: if get_segment_user_count becomes get_segment_size, an agent searching for segment user count still finds it, because matching happens on description rather than identifier.

The architecture in practice

The request flow from agent to internal API is short, and every layer has a specific job. Agent services connect through a VPC interface endpoint to AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates Cedar policies and routes tool calls through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to internal APIs.

The following diagram shows how the components connect.

Figure 1: MoEngage AgentCore Gateway architecture

An agent service running on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or in a container calls the MCP client. The client can be the official MCP SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, or MoEngage’s own agent runner. The client signs the request with SigV4 using the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role the service already has. The request travels over HTTPS to a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public hop. AgentCore Gateway receives the request and evaluates Cedar policies to determine what this principal can see or call. It then routes tool invocations through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to the internal API.

MoEngage made two authentication decisions worth calling out.

First, they chose SigV4 over JWT for the internal gateway. Agents here are services that already have IAM roles. With SigV4, they can sign with credentials they already have. Nothing new to issue, rotate, or store. MoEngage’s separate public MCP server, which serves human-authenticated sessions from Claude and other clients, uses OIDC JWTs on AgentCore runtime. That is a different surface with different requirements.

Second, identity travels as headers, not as tool arguments. Tenant, user, role, and database context are converted by the client library from a small Identity object into X-MOE-* headers. The model doesn’t see them and can’t set them. One detail matters for anyone building something similar: Because SigV4 signing occupies the Authorization header, caller-forwarded bearer tokens must move elsewhere. MoEngage propagates it as a dedicated MoEngage-prefixed header. Header propagation is also capped, so the set of headers is deliberate rather than accumulated.

Discovery and execution have different identity requirements. Listing and searching tools carries no tenant identity. Only tools/call does. That separation keeps discovery cheap and makes the audit trail unambiguous. Every identity-bearing request is an actual data access.

Even with Cedar scoping an agent to a subset of the catalog, the subset can be large. MoEngage’s client library exposes a single meta-tool, search_tools, to the model. The model describes what it needs, the gateway’s semantic search returns candidates, and only those candidates become callable for the rest of the turn. The full catalog doesn’t enter context. The agent’s context contains one tool definition at the start and a handful of relevant ones after a search, instead of several hundred definitions it will never use.

Onboarding a new API

A team exposing an API as an agent tool adds a block to its existing OpenAPI spec:

paths:
  /campaigns:
    get:
      operationId: listCampaigns
      description: |
        Returns a paginated list of campaigns. Supports filtering by
        status, channel, date range, and tags.
      x-moe-mcp:
        expose:
          external: false
          internal: true
        tool_description: |
          Find campaigns by status or channel. Returns campaign ID, name,
          status, and channel. Use the returned campaign_id with
          get_campaign for full details, or send_campaign to launch it.
        param_overrides:
          status:
            description: |
              Filter by campaign status. Use 'active' for running
              campaigns, 'scheduled' for upcoming. Omit for all.

Four design choices in that block are worth explaining.

Exposure is explicit opt-in. An endpoint with no x-moe-mcp block is not a tool. Continuous integration (CI) does not warn about its absence, because for most endpoints absence is the correct state. Cache-warmup routes and migration triggers are not agent tools, and nothing should nudge a team toward making them one. With the internal and external flags, a team can expose an operation to internal agents, to the public MCP server, or to both, independently.

Tool descriptions aren’t API descriptions. An API description tells a developer reading docs what an endpoint returns. A tool description tells a model when to reach for this tool and what to pass. MoEngage found that reusing API descriptions verbatim led to poor tool selection. Models picked tools based on implementation detail (“Returns a paginated list”) rather than intent (“Find campaigns by status or channel”). The tool_description and param_overrides fields exist specifically to give teams a place to write model-facing text without changing their developer-facing docs.

The CI pipeline handles everything from spec to running tool. When a team pushes a spec change, the pipeline validates the x-moe-mcp block, registers the target with AgentCore Gateway, and applies the Cedar policy. No manual steps, no tickets to the AI Platform team. A team that has never thought about MCP can have an operation available as an agent tool in the time it takes the pipeline to run.

The client library comes in two modes. A plug-in mode wraps the AgentCore Gateway MCP server inside LangChain, Google ADK, or an MCP-compatible framework as a tool provider. An agent runner mode runs a complete agent loop for teams that want a standalone agent without adopting a framework.

What MoEngage runs today

MoEngage’s AgentCore Gateway deployment runs in seven AWS Regions today. The gateway serves roughly 400 registered API operations to 10 internal agents. No product team has written MCP server code. No product team has provisioned networking for an agent integration. No product team has implemented Cedar policies. The AI Platform team owns all of that, and the cost of onboarding a new API is a spec annotation and a CI run. AgentCore feature availability varies by Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

The system has been running in production for three months. The agents span the workflow a marketing team member touches daily. A campaign QA agent validates targeting rules and content before launch. A delivery health agent monitors send rates and bounce patterns across channels. A segment builder agent translates natural-language audience descriptions into segment queries. Each agent authenticates with its own IAM role, sees only the tools its Cedar policy permits, and discovers tools by describing the task rather than memorizing tool names. By removing the need to build and operate 20 separate MCP servers and provision per-API networking across seven Regions, MoEngage estimates the approach saved approximately six months of engineering effort. Onboarding a new API now takes hours of spec annotation instead of days of networking provisioning and security review.

The search-first pattern changed how MoEngage thinks about agent design. New agents start with zero hardcoded tool references. They describe intent, receive candidates, and call what they find. When a team renames an operation or ships a new one, existing agents pick it up without a code change.

Conclusion

The key insight behind MoEngage’s approach is a separation of concerns that maps to how engineering organizations actually work. Product teams own APIs and describe them well. A platform team owns the protocol layer, the policy layer, and the connectivity layer. AgentCore Gateway made that split practical by removing the undifferentiated work in between: no MCP server code, no per-API networking, no client-side filtering pretending to be authorization.

The result is an agent system where adding a new tool is a spec change, restricting access is a policy change, and neither requires the other team to be involved.

To get started with AgentCore Gateway, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. For Cedar policy authoring, see the Cedar policy language reference. For private connectivity patterns, see the Amazon VPC Lattice documentation.

To discuss a similar architecture for your organization, contact your AWS account team or reach out to AWS.

 

About the authors

Nikhil is a Lead Software Engineer in the CTO’s office at MoEngage, where he leads the AI Labs team building agentic AI capabilities. His work spans MCP server and tool-catalog architecture, LLM gateway and routing infrastructure, and evaluating agent frameworks for both internal tooling and public agent experiences. He has over 4 years of experience building software and cloud infrastructure at scale.

Shakir is an Architect at MoEngage, where he leads API governance and builds core streaming infrastructure powering the company’s customer engagement platform. His work spans gateway architecture, real-time streaming with Flink and Kafka, and large-scale data migrations. He has over 11 years of experience designing systems that serve billions of customer interactions, including 5 years at MoEngage.

Bhupesh is a Principal Account Manager at Amazon Web Services, where he partners with independent software vendors (ISVs) to align their platform strategy with their business goals. He works with C-suite and senior leadership to accelerate growth, bring new capabilities to market, and turn technical investments into customer reach and differentiation.

Anant is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, where he works with ISV customers to design multi-tenant architectures and productionize AI-driven solutions. His areas of expertise include agentic AI, agent orchestration patterns, responsible AI, and helping product companies adopt generative AI on AWS. Outside of work, Anant is passionate about exploring how emerging AI paradigms reshape the way software products are built and delivered.

item.title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
item.dc:creator: Alex Iankoulski
item.description: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that pairs reasoning and tool use with multimodal understanding. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM.
item.content:encoded:
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Nano Omni, Super, Ultra, and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS.

About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details:

  • 120B total parameters, 12B active per token.
  • Hybrid Mamba-2, MoE, and attention layers with a RADIO vision encoder.
  • Context length up to 1M tokens.
  • Input: text, image, document, and video.
  • Output: text.
  • BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints.

NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. (technical report)

Model architecture

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding.

Use cases

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding:

  • Coding: test and validate code, analyze errors, recommend fixes.
  • Web research: cross-reference and verify sources returned by search tools.
  • Document intelligence: read tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries.
  • Cyber security: identify vulnerabilities and triage threats.
  • Video understanding: search, content, review, and incident analysis.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit. For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog.

Minimum GPU configurations

vLLM (GPU Model / min count) BF16 NVFP4
B200/GB200 8 2
B300/GB300 4 1
H200 8 4
H100 16 8

Deployment on AWS

This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family.

Deployment architecture

The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. The following figure shows a standard Amazon EKS cluster.

Figure 1: Standard Amazon EKS cluster architecture for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models

NVIDIA Dynamo serves the model aggregated on a single node or disaggregated with prefill and decode on different nodes. For vision-language models, the image/video encoding stage can in addition run disaggregated on its own node.

Validation and performance

This architecture has been validated on both p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA B200 GPUs) and p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) instances. You can validate the cluster and its network with an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce micro-benchmark.

Figure 2: GPU and EFA utilization during an NCCL all-reduce validation test

Seeing utilization on all GPUs and traffic on all EFA adapters while the NCCL test is running, verifies that the cluster is working as expected.

You can measure the performance of a deployed model on the cluster with the NVIDIA aiperf tool.

Figure 3: aiperf performance metrics for the deployed model

The aiperf output in the upper left pane shows key performance indicators (KPIs) like time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput in tokens per second (TPS). By taking these measurements at various levels of concurrency, we can study how latency and throughput depend on the number of concurrent requests. This information is essential to thoughtfully plan capacity and model deployment topology. The aws-do-eks container provides automation for visualizing GPU and EFA utilization as well as running aiperf and concurrency sweeps with single commands.

Figure 4: Concurrency sweep comparing aggregated and disaggregated deployments

The preceding concurrency sweep diagram reveals that the inference of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has lower TTFT and about the same ITL between aggregated and disaggregated deployments on two nodes.

A chart like this is useful when making deployment decisions. Draw your latency budget as horizontal lines, for example TTFT under 600 ms (about 1 second) and ITL under 100 ms per token. The rightmost point under both lines is the throughput one replica of this topology can serve within the service level objective (SLO), here c32, or about 320 tokens per second. To plan capacity, divide your target tokens per second by this per-replica throughput and find the number of prefill-decode pairs to deploy. Re-running the same sweep after a change (precision, TP/PP shape, aggregated versus disaggregated, a new Dynamo or vLLM release) makes the trade-off visible immediately. A curve that moves right and down is a win. Because TTFT and ITL are plotted separately, it also tells you which side to scale: rising ITL says add decode capacity, and rising TTFT says add prefill capacity.

Conclusion

This post covers the architecture and performance evaluation patterns for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM. To get started, deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in your own account, using the reference implementation. More inference blueprints are also available in the AI on EKS project. To get further hands-on experience with inference on EKS, register for our upcoming workshops.

item.title: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Omar Elkharbotly
item.description: Stand up a governed, multi-account Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This post walks through the architecture and an open-source reference blueprint: the operating model, control plane, per-Workstream cells, separate inference and tool gateways, and a CI/CD evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before production.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve tried to get an agent into production, the model and tool use are not the blocker. The main bottleneck is everything around them: how many teams can build within a secure environment, which team owns each model and tool, how AgentOps and error handling stay inside a pre-defined boundary, and how platform, Workstream, and finance teams see cost and health across accounts. For a Platform team that wants to support many agentic use cases, that’s a platform product to design and operate. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Workstream teams. Workstream teams are the domain or product teams that build and own agents on the platform.

Each Workstream team needs a paved road with approved models and tools, short-lived workload identity, isolated runtime and memory, automated evaluation, rollback, telemetry, and cost attribution. These controls need to remain consistent as Workstream teams customize prompts, tools, data access, and application behavior. When every team assembles them, controls drift, shared services become a bottleneck, and ownership is difficult to audit.

In this post, we walk through the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover the multi-account operating model, the Platform control plane, a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern, separate inference and tool gateways, and an evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before promotion to production. By the end, you should be able to deploy a governed Workstream from the companion blueprint, validate its security and lifecycle contracts, and use it as the foundation for your own agentic AI platform in the organization.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular services for building, deploying, and operating agents at scale, including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations. The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint, built on AgentCore, adds the surrounding enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code: ownership, account boundaries, software delivery, observability, cost governance, and retirement.

Architectural principles

Before diving into the solution details, it helps to understand the organizational needs that drive the platform architecture. The common challenges we have heard from customers who establish an agent platform fall into these five categories:

  1. Governed model access: Every untrusted inference request must pass through an approved inference gateway. The gateway applies the organization’s guardrails (for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails or a third-party provider), restricts which models and inference AWS Regions each Workstream can use, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits, token quotas, and budgets so that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. It also carries workload identity and emits attribution data.
  2. Governed tool access: Agents must discover and invoke only approved tools through an authenticated Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, with exact targets, least-privilege execution roles, policy decisions, and an auditable owner.
  3. Delegated delivery: Workstream teams (for example, product teams) need to ship and roll back independently inside pre-approved boundaries, without waiting for the platform team to deploy each application or granting developers a direct infrastructure write path.
  4. Fleet operations and cost: Several personas need visibility across accounts without gaining write access to team workloads. Agent operations engineers need logs, metrics, traces, and quotas. Workstream owners need cost per agent against their budgets. FinOps and finance teams need chargeback by team or business unit through AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Security and governance leads need evidence of which workload called which model and tool.
  5. Bounded evidence and lifecycle: Every agent release needs proof at each boundary it touches:
    1. Model access: An approved model call succeeds, and a call to an unapproved model or Region is denied.
    2. Tool access: A subscribed tool call succeeds, and a call to a tool outside the agent’s subscription is denied with the expected error.
    3. Identity: A request from another workstream’s account or identity is rejected.
    4. Release: The previous agent runtime version can be restored.
    5. Retirement: Teardown removes the agent’s runtime, memory, tool gateway, and tool grants in dependency order, and confirms nothing is left behind.

The blueprint addresses these needs through four connected planes: developer experience, platform control, Workstream execution, and assurance and operations. The unit of scale is the Workstream cell, not a manually configured agent or one shared workload account. The blueprint README documents the responsibilities of each plane in detail. And you will read the main planes: Agentic AI Platform control plane and Repeatable Workstream cell in the later paragraphs.

Operating models and platform components

Enterprises usually adopt one of three operating models for agentic AI:

  • Centralized: A single artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) team builds and runs every agent. Governance is consistent, but that team quickly becomes a bottleneck as the number of use cases grows.
  • Decentralized: Each business unit builds and operates its own agents. Teams can move quickly, but without shared standards, controls tend to drift, effort gets duplicated, and cost visibility suffers.
  • Federated: A central Platform team provides shared, governed services while domain teams retain ownership of their agents, tools, and data. This model balances team autonomy with consistent guardrails and is where most enterprises land.
  • For assistance choosing, see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance page on Governance Models.

Following patterns we have observed in customer engagements, the blueprint implements the federated model. The Platform team is the hub, typically a Platform product manager, architect, platform engineers, agent operations engineers, and a security and governance lead. Workstream teams are the spokes, made up of agent developers, a domain tech lead, and AI/ML engineers. An executive sponsor and the CISO sit above both.

In this blueprint, the Platform team owns the definition of each component: templates, versions, policies, and admission. Each Workstream account runs its own instance of the per-team components (Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway), so a failure or rollback stays inside one team’s boundary.

Solution overview

This solution delivers a governed, multi-account Agentic AI Platform that platform teams operate, and workstream teams such as internal product and engineering teams consume through versioned, self-service interfaces.

At enterprise scale, the developer experience plane is a catalog of organization-approved, versioned agent templates. The blueprint ships reference templates for Strands, LangGraph, and CrewAI, but you can use your choice of framework when the template preserves the same inference gateway, tool gateway, identity, policy, evaluation, and delivery contracts. Application teams own prompts, agent logic, tools, and evaluation cases. The Platform team owns the common controls and release requirements.

Out of the four planes, two carry most of the architecture:

  1. Agentic AI Platform control plane: The Platform account publishes versioned templates and interfaces, operates AWS Agent Registry governance records and shared Inference Gateways, admits models and Guardrails, orchestrates reviewed releases, and aggregates fleet signals. Teams consume these capabilities through code, descriptors, and pipelines rather than administrator sessions or deployment tickets.
  2. Repeatable Workstream cell: Each product or domain receives an isolated boundary with a team-owned source repository, a Workload pipeline, and three Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities: AgentCore Runtime, actor-scoped AgentCore Memory, and an AgentCore Gateway that uses AWS_IAM authorization and exposes only the approved tool targets. The cell also holds local customer managed AWS KMS keys, tags, alarms, budgets, and a CloudWatch Observability Access Manager (OAM) source link. One cell can deploy, fail, roll back, or retire without coordinating with another team’s release.

Key components

The following diagram illustrates the operating model and governed flow of the solution.

Figure 1: Enterprise Agentic AI Platform operating model, showing the governance foundation, the Platform control plane, repeatable team-owned Workstream cells, and the software delivery, inference, tool, telemetry, and ownership flows between them.

The architecture consists of the following account layers:

  1. Management and governance foundation. AWS Organizations, AWS IAM Identity Center, preventive policy, audit, retention, and cost policy establish the enterprise boundary. These are logical responsibilities that can map to an existing AWS Control Tower landing zone rather than requiring a duplicate account structure.
  2. Security, audit, and observability layer. AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, log archive, and an Amazon CloudWatch OAM sink provide independent control-plane evidence and fleet visibility. Central operators can query shared signals without gaining write access to Workstream resources.
  3. Platform layer of Agentic AI Platform. Separate Platform environments own golden paths, the governance catalog, Guardrails, shared Inference Gateways, exact tool aliases, pipelines, compatibility, quotas, and common operational interfaces. Platform changes are tested against representative cells before wider rollout.
  4. Workstream fleet layer. Each product, domain, or regulated boundary receives one or more nonproduction and production cells. Teams own Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, tools, data, prompts, evaluation cases, application incidents, and service-level objectives (SLOs). The same baseline can be repeated across many cells while preserving account-level isolation.

Solution walkthrough

The following sections trace the key design decisions: account topology, preventive and detective controls, the AgentCore execution path, and the delivery pipeline.

Account topology and organizational units

The blueprint defines logical account roles that separate enterprise governance, shared Platform services, and team-owned execution:

Role Landing-zone placement Purpose
Management foundation Root / Security and Management Organizations, Identity Center, preventive policy, audit, retention, and cost policy
Security and log archive Security CloudTrail, AWS Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, and retained audit data
Observability Security or Operations CloudWatch OAM sink and fleet logs, metrics, traces, and cost views
Agentic AI Platform Agent Platform Golden paths, AWS Agent Registry, Guardrails, Inference Gateways, pipelines, and fleet controls
Workstream cell Agent Workstreams Team-owned Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, tools, data, evaluation, and application SLOs
Additional Workstream cells Agent Workstreams Repeat the same baseline per product, domain, environment, or regulated boundary

This topology integrates into an existing landing zone, a pre-configured, secure, and scalable multi-account AWS environment, where the Management, Platform, and Workstream labels describe responsibilities rather than a fixed three-account estate. An organization can operate multiple validated Platform environments and many Workstream account pairs. Start with one representative cell and prove onboarding, production promotion, rollback, centralized observability, and zero-residual retirement before repeating the baseline.

Service control policies

Service control policies constrain the maximum permissions available to Platform and Workstream accounts. They complement, rather than replace, IAM, gateway authorization, Guardrails, resource policies, network controls, and pipeline evidence. The blueprint renders and reviews the effective policies for the exact account and Region instead of relying on source-code intent alone.

  1. Model and Region admission: Organization policy and Gateway execution roles restrict inference to approved models and the supported Region. Adding a model or Region requires service availability, residency, IAM, quality, cost, rollback, observability, and denial validation.
  2. Guardrail and inference enforcement: Agents do not call model providers directly. Inference crosses the governed gateway, where the stage Guardrail and model allow-list are applied.
  3. Pipeline-only Workstream mutation: Workstream teams open pull requests and use the Workload pipeline. Direct developer deployment into Workstream accounts is outside the supported operating model, which keeps the reviewed release and evidence path non-bypassable.
  4. Registry and Gateway governance: Workstream Gateway synthesis fails when a subscribed Registry record is missing, changed, or not approved.
  5. Scoped deployment roles: Bootstrap policies are generated per account and Region, validated with AWS Identity and Access Management Access (IAM) Analyzer, and checked through effective-policy simulation. Administrator access is reserved for initial setup rather than routine pipeline execution.
  6. Separation of duties and adversarial proof: Platform controls model, Guardrail, Registry, and shared-service admission. Workstream teams control application behavior. Every denied path is paired with an authorized positive call and a mutation that proves the intended control caused the denial.

An administrator inside a Workstream account can’t create a supported fast path around these controls. New or changed organization policies need a sandbox or representative-cell soak, exact allow and deny tests, and a rollback plan before broad attachment.

CI/CD pipeline with evaluation gates

The blueprint uses reviewed Platform and Workload pipelines to enforce the following promotion sequence:

  1. Source and review: A pull request establishes the immutable source revision. The pipeline pins the intended branch so an unmerged change can’t silently build the repository default branch.
  2. Build and synth: The pipeline compiles code, runs tests and linting, creates the agent manifest, scans the digest-bound image, validates policies, resolves approved Registry descriptors, and inspects synthesized AWS CloudFormation and cdk-nag output.
  3. Stable roles and permission handoff: The Workload pipeline creates stable Workstream roles and pauses. The Platform pipeline grants exact tool aliases to the exact Gateway role, live policies are verified, and only then does the Workload pipeline continue.
  4. Deploy to nonproduction: The pipeline deploys Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, observability, alarms, budgets, tags, and application resources into the cell’s nonproduction boundary.
  5. Evaluate the deployed agent: The gate invokes the real Runtime and measures regression, quality, tool success, refusal behavior, first-token latency, and cost. Every authorized call is paired with an adversarial twin: the gate calls an approved model and confirms success, then calls an unapproved model and confirms the denial. The same pattern applies to tools, cross-account identity, and throttling. If an expected denial is missing, the gate fails the build.
  6. Human approval: A reviewer examines the deployed evidence, known limitations, and residual risk. A generic green build is not enough when a required probe, resource, or expected denial is missing.
  7. Promote, observe, and roll back: Production promotion uses the reviewed revision and continuity checks. Runtime sessions are sampled through update, cancellation, rollback, restore, and re-run so the pipeline proves both the forward path and recovery path.

No Workstream deployment step has a manual fast track. The Platform team owns the release contract, but Workstream teams operate their own pipeline instances and deployment cadence. Retirement follows a strict dependency order: Platform alias grants are revoked first, then Workstream Gateway and tool roles, then Runtime, Memory, and application resources. Each step is verified before proceeding, and a final inventory confirms zero residual resources remain.

Security and governance

The blueprint implements defense in depth through reinforcing identity, policy, delivery, data, and evidence controls:

  1. Identity and trust boundaries: AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito provide short-lived inference credentials. AWS_IAM and SigV4 authenticate tool traffic. Exact Runtime and Gateway roles, issuer and audience checks, account and Region context, and scoped bootstrap trust limit each principal to its intended path.
  2. Model safety and admission: Inference flows through the governed gateway described in the Solution overview, applying Guardrails and model allow-lists before every call.
  3. Tool authorization: The Tool Gateway invokes only Registry-approved aliases, as detailed in the Solution overview. Cedar policies provide authorization, with a retained AWS Lambda wrapper for defense in depth.
  4. Tenant data protection: Workstream accounts isolate application state. AgentCore memory uses actor-scoped namespaces and customer-managed KMS keys. Tools and application data remain team-owned, and retention, deletion, and access policies are explicit rather than inherited from a shared mutable workload account.
  5. Software supply chain and release: Reviewed source, manifest hashing, reproducible builds, digest-bound image scanning, policy validation, cdk-nag checks, deployed-runtime evaluation, human approval, rollback, and dependency-ordered teardown form one release contract. A missing check fails closed.
  6. Audit, observability, and cost governance: CloudTrail and retained control-plane data corroborate pipeline evidence. OAM shares logs, metrics, and traces with central operators. Standard allocation tags, budgets, quotas, and AWS Cost and Usage Report reconciliation assign ownership without giving the agent permission to rewrite its own attribution.

The repository is a reference implementation. Developers can adjust it to address their needs. The deployment and available features are based on the eu-west-1 (Ireland) Region. A substituted component, another Region, or a wider organizational rollout requires its own availability, security, load, rollback, observability, and teardown evidence.

Conclusion

In this post, we walked through an enterprise Agentic AI Platform built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture separates a centrally governed Platform control plane from repeatable, team-owned Workstream cells, with distinct inference and tool gateways, and production promotion gated by deployed-runtime evaluation.

The companion repository includes a blueprint that validates these controls end to end, from pipeline gates and adversarial boundary tests through zero-residual teardown. The support claim stops at that tested boundary.

To get started, deploy one representative Workstream cell from the companion repository, prove its full lifecycle, and then automate additional cells from the same versioned baseline.

  1. Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint on GitHub
  2. Enterprise multi-account architecture for running agentic AI in production on AWS (Prescriptive Guidance)
  3. Building an Enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Workshop
  4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation

Mia is a Specialist Solutions Architect for Agentic AI, based in Berlin, Germany. She helps enterprise customers across EMEA design, operationalize, and scale agentic AI workloads, from first agents to production on managed platforms; and hybrid architectures with self-managed infrastructure. Her expertise spans agentic application architecture, agent security and governance, Responsible AI, and platform engineering.
